Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

70. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors

A nonzero vector v\mathbf{v}v is an eigenvector of a square matrix AAA if multiplying by AAA only scales it:

Av=λvA\mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}Av=λv

The scale factor λ\lambdaλ is the eigenvalue. Eigenvectors are the directions a linear map stretches without turning, and they describe its long-run behavior when applied repeatedly.

71. The characteristic polynomial

The eigenvalues are the roots of det⁡(A−λI)=0\det(A - \lambda I) = 0det(A−λI)=0. For A=[2112]A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}A=[21​12​] this is (2−λ)2−1=0(2 - \lambda)^2 - 1 = 0(2−λ)2−1=0, so λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1 and λ=3\lambda = 3λ=3. This is a hand-calculation tool; numerical software computes eigenvalues with iterative algorithms instead of finding polynomial roots.

72. Eigendecomposition (diagonalization)

If an n×nn \times nn×n matrix has nnn independent eigenvectors, collected as the columns of VVV, then

A=VΛV−1A = V \Lambda V^{-1}A=VΛV−1

with the eigenvalues on the diagonal of Λ\LambdaΛ. Powers become easy, Ak=VΛkV−1A^k = V\Lambda^kV^{-1}Ak=VΛkV−1, which explains why repeated multiplication is dominated by the largest eigenvalues, a key idea behind exploding and vanishing gradients in recurrent networks.

73. The spectral theorem

A real symmetric matrix always has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal set of eigenvectors, so

A=QΛQ⊤A = Q \Lambda Q^\topA=QΛQ⊤

with QQQ orthogonal. Covariance matrices are symmetric, which is what makes PCA (entry 82) work so cleanly.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
eigenvalues, Q = np.linalg.eigh(A)   # eigh is for symmetric matrices
print(eigenvalues)
print(np.allclose(Q @ np.diag(eigenvalues) @ Q.T, A))

[1. 3.]
True

74. Positive definite and semidefinite matrices

A symmetric matrix AAA is positive definite if x⊤Ax>0\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x} > 0x⊤Ax>0 for every nonzero x\mathbf{x}x (equivalently, all eigenvalues are positive), and positive semidefinite if x⊤Ax≥0\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x} \ge 0x⊤Ax≥0. Covariance matrices and Gram matrices X⊤XX^\top XX⊤X are always positive semidefinite, and a valid kernel in a support vector machine must produce positive semidefinite kernel matrices.

75. Cholesky decomposition

A positive definite matrix factors as A=LL⊤A = LL^\topA=LL⊤ with LLL lower triangular. Cholesky is about twice as fast as LU, and it is the standard way to sample from a multivariate Gaussian: if z\mathbf{z}z has independent standard-normal entries and Σ=LL⊤\Sigma = LL^\topΣ=LL⊤, then μ+Lz\boldsymbol{\mu} + L\mathbf{z}μ+Lz has mean μ\boldsymbol{\mu}μ and covariance Σ\SigmaΣ. Gaussian-process libraries also rely on it.

76. Power iteration

Multiplying a vector by AAA over and over, and renormalizing each time, converges (under mild conditions) to the eigenvector with the largest-magnitude eigenvalue. This power iteration is simple enough to run on enormous sparse matrices, and it is the classic way to compute PageRank-style scores on a link graph.

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2.0, 1.0], [1.0, 2.0]])
v = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
for _ in range(50):
    v = A @ v
    v = v / np.linalg.norm(v)
print(np.round(v, 4), round(v @ A @ v, 4))   # eigenvector and its eigenvalue

[0.7071 0.7071] 3.0

77. Markov chains and stationary distributions

A Markov chain with transition matrix PPP (each row sums to 1) has a stationary distribution π\boldsymbol{\pi}π with π⊤P=π⊤\boldsymbol{\pi}^\top P = \boldsymbol{\pi}^\topπ⊤P=π⊤, which is a left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. Long-run behavior in random-walk models, MCMC samplers and PageRank is governed by this eigenvector.

SVD, PCA and dimensionality reduction

78. Singular value decomposition (SVD)

Every real m×nm \times nm×n matrix, square or not, factors as

A=UΣV⊤A = U \Sigma V^\topA=UΣV⊤

where UUU and VVV have orthonormal columns and Σ\SigmaΣ is diagonal with nonnegative singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥0\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge 0σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥0. Equivalently, A=∑iσiuivi⊤A = \sum_i \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\topA=∑i​σi​ui​vi⊤​, a sum of rank-1 pieces ordered by importance. NumPy's np.linalg.svd returns U, S and Vh (that is, V⊤V^\topV⊤), with the singular values sorted in descending order.

79. The geometry of the SVD

The SVD says every linear map is a rotation (or reflection) V⊤V^\topV⊤, followed by stretching each axis by σi\sigma_iσi​, followed by another rotation UUU. The largest singular value is the most any unit vector can be stretched, and the number of nonzero singular values is the rank.

80. Truncated SVD and the best low-rank approximation

Keeping only the top kkk singular values gives

Ak=∑i=1kσiuivi⊤A_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\topAk​=i=1∑k​σi​ui​vi⊤​

By the Eckart–Young theorem, AkA_kAk​ is the closest rank-kkk matrix to AAA in both the Frobenius and spectral norms, and the Frobenius error is σk+12+⋯\sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \cdots}σk+12​+⋯​. This underlies image compression demos, latent semantic analysis and many model-compression methods.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.normal(size=(6, 4))
U, S, Vh = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
k = 2
A_k = (U[:, :k] * S[:k]) @ Vh[:k, :]
print(np.isclose(np.linalg.norm(A - A_k), np.sqrt(np.sum(S[k:] ** 2))))

True

81. The covariance matrix

For a data matrix XXX whose columns have been centered (mean subtracted), the sample covariance matrix is

C=1m−1X⊤XC = \frac{1}{m - 1} X^\top XC=m−11​X⊤X

Entry CijC_{ij}Cij​ is the covariance between features iii and jjj, and the diagonal holds the variances. It is symmetric and positive semidefinite.

82. Principal component analysis (PCA)

PCA finds the orthogonal directions along which the centered data vary most. They are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, or equivalently the right singular vectors of the centered data matrix, and projecting onto the top kkk of them gives the best kkk-dimensional linear summary of the data in the squared-error sense. Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong) devotes a full chapter to deriving it.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
t = rng.normal(size=200)
X = np.column_stack([t, 2 * t + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=200)])   # nearly 1-D data
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
_, S, Vh = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
explained = S**2 / np.sum(S**2)
print(np.round(np.abs(Vh[0]), 3), np.round(explained, 4))

[0.446 0.895] [9.996e-01 4.000e-04]

83. Explained variance

The variance captured by principal component iii is proportional to σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​ (or to the covariance eigenvalue λi\lambda_iλi​), so the explained variance ratio is σi2/∑jσj2\sigma_i^2 / \sum_j \sigma_j^2σi2​/∑j​σj2​. In the example above, the first component explains almost all of the variance because the data lie close to a line. Choosing kkk so that the cumulative ratio passes a threshold such as 95% is a common heuristic, not a rule.

84. Whitening

Whitening transforms data so its covariance becomes the identity: rotate onto the principal axes, then divide each coordinate by its standard deviation, z=Λ−1/2Q⊤(x−μ)\mathbf{z} = \Lambda^{-1/2} Q^\top(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})z=Λ−1/2Q⊤(x−μ). Whitened features are uncorrelated with unit variance, which can make some learning algorithms better conditioned. Directions with tiny variance get hugely amplified, so a small constant is usually added to the eigenvalues first.

85. Matrix factorization for recommendations

A user–item rating matrix RRR (users by items) can be approximated as R≈UV⊤R \approx UV^\topR≈UV⊤, where each row of UUU is a user's vector of latent factors and each row of VVV is an item's. A predicted rating is a dot product ui⊤vj\mathbf{u}_i^\top \mathbf{v}_jui⊤​vj​. Because most ratings are missing, the factors are fitted only to observed entries, usually with gradient descent or alternating least squares rather than a plain SVD.

86. The spectral norm

The spectral norm ∥A∥2=σmax⁡(A)\lVert A \rVert_2 = \sigma_{\max}(A)∥A∥2​=σmax​(A) is the largest factor by which AAA can stretch a vector. A layer x↦Wx\mathbf{x} \mapsto W\mathbf{x}x↦Wx is Lipschitz with constant ∥W∥2\lVert W \rVert_2∥W∥2​, so constraining spectral norms bounds how sensitive a network is to input changes. Spectral normalization, used to stabilize GAN discriminators, divides each weight matrix by an estimate of its spectral norm (computed with power iteration, entry 76).

Matrix calculus for training models

87. The gradient

For a scalar function f(x)f(\mathbf{x})f(x) of a vector, the gradient collects all partial derivatives:

∇f(x)=(∂f∂x1,…,∂f∂xn)\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \dots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \right)∇f(x)=(∂x1​∂f​,…,∂xn​∂f​)

It points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length is the rate of increase in that direction. Training a model means following the negative gradient of the loss.

88. Two gradients worth memorizing

Two identities cover a surprising amount of machine learning:

∇x x⊤Ax=(A+A⊤)x,∇w∥Xw−y∥22=2X⊤(Xw−y)\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\, \mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x} = (A + A^\top)\mathbf{x}, \qquad \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \lVert X\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y} \rVert_2^2 = 2X^\top(X\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y})∇x​x⊤Ax=(A+A⊤)x,∇w​∥Xw−y∥22​=2X⊤(Xw−y)

For symmetric AAA the first becomes 2Ax2A\mathbf{x}2Ax. Setting the second to zero gives the normal equations (entry 65).

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
X, y, w = rng.normal(size=(5, 3)), rng.normal(size=5), rng.normal(size=3)
loss = lambda w: np.sum((X @ w - y) ** 2)
analytic = 2 * X.T @ (X @ w - y)
h = 1e-6
numeric = np.array([(loss(w + h * e) - loss(w - h * e)) / (2 * h) for e in np.eye(3)])
print(np.allclose(analytic, numeric, atol=1e-5))

True

89. The Jacobian

For a vector-valued function f:Rn→Rm\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^mf:Rn→Rm, the Jacobian is the m×nm \times nm×n matrix of partial derivatives Jij=∂fi/∂xjJ_{ij} = \partial f_i / \partial x_jJij​=∂fi​/∂xj​. It is the best linear approximation of f\mathbf{f}f near a point: f(x+δ)≈f(x)+Jδ\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\delta}) \approx \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) + J\boldsymbol{\delta}f(x+δ)≈f(x)+Jδ. For a linear layer f(x)=Wx\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) = W\mathbf{x}f(x)=Wx, the Jacobian is simply WWW.

90. The Hessian

The Hessian of a scalar function is the symmetric matrix of second derivatives, Hij=∂2f/∂xi∂xjH_{ij} = \partial^2 f / \partial x_i \partial x_jHij​=∂2f/∂xi​∂xj​. Its eigenvalues describe the curvature of the loss surface: large eigenvalues mean steep, narrow valleys where a big learning rate overshoots, and mixed-sign eigenvalues mean a saddle point. For least squares, the Hessian is the constant matrix 2X⊤X2X^\top X2X⊤X.

91. The chain rule as Jacobian products (backpropagation)

For a composition y=f(g(x))\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}))y=f(g(x)), the Jacobians multiply: Jy,x=Jf JgJ_{\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}} = J_{\mathbf{f}} \, J_{\mathbf{g}}Jy,x​=Jf​Jg​. Backpropagation evaluates this product from the loss backward, multiplying a row vector (the gradient so far) by one Jacobian at a time. That ordering is far cheaper than forming the full Jacobian matrices, because each step is a vector–matrix product rather than a matrix–matrix product.

92. Gradient descent

Gradient descent repeatedly updates the parameters with

w←w−η ∇wL(w)\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta \, \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})w←w−η∇w​L(w)

where η\etaη is the learning rate. For a quadratic loss the method converges only if η<2/λmax⁡\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}η<2/λmax​, where λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​ is the largest Hessian eigenvalue, and it converges slowly when the condition number of the Hessian is large. Optimizers such as momentum and Adam were designed largely to cope with this ill-conditioning.

93. Convexity and positive semidefinite Hessians

A twice-differentiable function is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere. Convex losses, such as least squares, ridge and logistic regression, have no bad local minima, so gradient descent can reach the global minimum. Deep network losses are not convex, which is one reason their training behavior is harder to analyze.

Tensors and efficient computation

94. Tensor shapes in deep learning

Most deep learning bugs are shape bugs, so it pays to name every axis. A transformer's hidden states typically have shape (batch,sequence,dmodel)(\text{batch}, \text{sequence}, d_\text{model})(batch,sequence,dmodel​), image batches are (batch,channels,height,width)(\text{batch}, \text{channels}, \text{height}, \text{width})(batch,channels,height,width) in PyTorch's default layout, and attention scores have shape (batch,heads,sequence,sequence)(\text{batch}, \text{heads}, \text{sequence}, \text{sequence})(batch,heads,sequence,sequence).

95. Broadcasting

Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes combine without copying data. NumPy compares shapes from the last axis backward; two dimensions are compatible when they are equal or one of them is 1, and missing leading dimensions count as 1. Adding a bias vector to every row of a batch is the classic case; Deep Learning (Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville) describes the same convention for adding a vector to a matrix.

import numpy as np

X = np.arange(6.0).reshape(3, 2)   # 3 examples, 2 features
mu = X.mean(axis=0)                # shape (2,)
print(X - mu)                      # (3, 2) - (2,) broadcasts over rows

[[-2. -2.]
 [ 0.  0.]
 [ 2.  2.]]

96. Einstein summation (einsum)

einsum names each axis with a letter and sums over letters that disappear from the output. It expresses many linear algebra operations in one readable line: "ij,j->i" is a matrix-vector product, "ij,jk->ik" a matrix product, "bqd,bkd->bqk" a batched set of all query–key dot products.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
Q = rng.normal(size=(2, 4, 8))   # batch, queries, dim
K = rng.normal(size=(2, 5, 8))   # batch, keys, dim
scores = np.einsum("bqd,bkd->bqk", Q, K)
print(scores.shape, np.allclose(scores, Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1)))

(2, 4, 5) True

97. The cost of matrix multiplication

Multiplying an m×km \times km×k matrix by a k×nk \times nk×n matrix takes mnkmnkmnk multiply–add pairs, usually counted as 2mnk2mnk2mnk floating-point operations. A single 4096×40964096 \times 40964096×4096 by 4096×40964096 \times 40964096×4096 product is therefore about 1.4×10111.4 \times 10^{11}1.4×1011 operations. Because matrix products dominate the cost of training and running neural networks, hardware accelerators are built around fast matrix multiplication.

Linear algebra inside modern AI models

98. Scaled dot-product attention

The core of the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) is a few matrix products:

Attention⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡ ⁣(QK⊤dk)V\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right) VAttention(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V

Each row of QK⊤QK^\topQK⊤ holds one query's dot products with every key (entry 19), softmax turns each row into weights that sum to 1, and multiplying by VVV takes weighted averages of the value vectors. The paper explains the 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_k}1/dk​​ factor: if query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance dkd_kdk​, and large dot products push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients.

import numpy as np

def attention(Q, K, V):
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[-1])
    scores = scores - scores.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)   # stable softmax
    weights = np.exp(scores)
    weights = weights / weights.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return weights @ V, weights

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
Q, K, V = rng.normal(size=(3, 8)), rng.normal(size=(5, 8)), rng.normal(size=(5, 16))
out, weights = attention(Q, K, V)
print(out.shape, np.allclose(weights.sum(axis=1), 1.0))

(3, 16) True

99. Multi-head attention

Instead of one attention operation, multi-head attention projects the inputs with several learned matrices and runs attention in parallel in each projected subspace:

MultiHead⁡(Q,K,V)=Concat⁡(head1,…,headh) WO,headi=Attention⁡(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV)\operatorname{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)\,W^{O}, \qquad \text{head}_i = \operatorname{Attention}(QW_i^{Q}, KW_i^{K}, VW_i^{V})MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1​,…,headh​)WO,headi​=Attention(QWiQ​,KWiK​,VWiV​)

The base model in the original paper used dmodel=512d_\text{model} = 512dmodel​=512 and h=8h = 8h=8 heads, so each head works in a dk=64d_k = 64dk​=64-dimensional subspace. Each head is free to attend to different relationships, and all of it is still just matrix multiplication.

100. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA)

LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) fine-tunes a large model by freezing a pretrained weight matrix W0∈Rd×kW_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}W0​∈Rd×k and learning a low-rank update:

h=W0x+ΔW x=W0x+BA x,B∈Rd×r,  A∈Rr×k,  r≪min⁡(d,k)\mathbf{h} = W_0\mathbf{x} + \Delta W\,\mathbf{x} = W_0\mathbf{x} + BA\,\mathbf{x}, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, \; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}, \; r \ll \min(d, k)h=W0​x+ΔWx=W0​x+BAx,B∈Rd×r,A∈Rr×k,r≪min(d,k)

AAA starts as random Gaussian and BBB as zero, so the update is zero at the start of training, and the update is scaled by α/r\alpha / rα/r. For a 4096×40964096 \times 40964096×4096 matrix with r=8r = 8r=8, BBB and AAA together hold 8×(4096+4096)=65,5368 \times (4096 + 4096) = 65{,}5368×(4096+4096)=65,536 trainable numbers instead of about 16.8 million. The paper reports up to 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning of GPT-3 175B.

101. Numerical precision and stability

Real computations use floating-point numbers, so algebraically equal formulas can give different answers. A few habits prevent most problems: subtract the maximum before exponentiating in softmax (as in entry 98), solve systems instead of inverting (entry 47), prefer QR or SVD over normal equations for ill-conditioned problems (entry 69), and compare floats with tolerances (np.allclose) rather than ==. Lower-precision formats such as float16 and bfloat16 make these habits even more important.

import numpy as np

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, np.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
z = np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    naive = np.exp(z) / np.exp(z).sum()
stable = np.exp(z - z.max()) / np.exp(z - z.max()).sum()
print(naive, np.round(stable, 4))

False True
[nan nan nan] [0.09   0.2447 0.6652]

Common mistakes

  • Confusing * with @. In NumPy and PyTorch, * is the element-wise (Hadamard) product and @ is matrix multiplication (entries 25 and 30).
  • Mixing up the two meanings of "rank". A tensor's number of axes and a matrix's linear-algebra rank are different things (entries 1 and 51).
  • Computing inverses to solve systems. Use a solver or least-squares routine instead (entries 47 and 66).
  • Forgetting to center data before PCA. Without subtracting the mean, the first component mostly points at the mean rather than along the direction of greatest variance (entry 82).
  • Comparing raw distances between unscaled features. Standardize first, or the feature with the largest units dominates (entry 16).
  • Assuming that a small error in the inputs means a small error in the output. Check the condition number when results look unstable (entry 69).

Next steps

  • Practice the algebra behind these ideas with 150 algebra problems with solutions.
  • Keep the core identities at hand with 100 mathematics formulas every student should know.
  • See where covariance, regression and hypothesis tests show up in practice in 100 probability and statistics examples.
  • Speed up hand calculations with 101 math tricks to solve problems faster.
  • Browse more writing on mathematics and engineering, including external blogs in the community directory.

References

  1. Deisenroth, M. P., Faisal, A. A., & Ong, C. S. (2020). Mathematics for Machine Learning. Cambridge University Press. Free PDF: mml-book.github.io
  2. Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., & Courville, A. (2016). Deep Learning, Chapter 2: Linear Algebra. MIT Press. deeplearningbook.org
  3. Strang, G. 18.06SC Linear Algebra (Fall 2011). MIT OpenCourseWare. ocw.mit.edu
  4. Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., et al. (2017). "Attention Is All You Need." arXiv:1706.03762. arxiv.org
  5. Hu, E. J., Shen, Y., Wallis, P., et al. (2021). "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models." arXiv:2106.09685. arxiv.org
  6. Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). "Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space." arXiv:1301.3781. arxiv.org
  7. Cook, J. D. (2010, January 19). "Don't invert that matrix." johndcook.com
  8. NumPy Developers. "Broadcasting." NumPy documentation. numpy.org
  9. NumPy Developers. "numpy.linalg.svd" and "numpy.linalg.lstsq." NumPy documentation. numpy.org

title: 100 Best Mathematics Formulas Every Student Should Know
description: The 100 formulas students use most, from algebra and geometry to calculus, statistics and vectors, each with symbols explained and a worked example.
author: BlogAI Editors
html:
This is a working reference for the formulas that come up again and again in school and early university mathematics: algebra, exponents and logarithms, geometry, coordinate geometry, trigonometry, sequences, calculus, probability and statistics, and vectors and matrices.

Each of the 100 entries gives the formula, what every symbol means, when to reach for it, and a short worked example. Use the sections as a checklist. If you cannot say when a formula applies, or you cannot redo its example without looking, that is the one to practise. Each formula was checked against the open textbooks and reference pages listed under References, and every worked example was recomputed numerically.

Arithmetic and algebra

These are the algebra results that save the most time when solving equations and simplifying expressions (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, sections 1.4, 1.5, 2.5 and 5.1; Prealgebra 2e, sections 6.2 and 6.4).

1. Quadratic formula

x=−b±b2−4ac2ax = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

Symbols: aaa, bbb and ccc are the coefficients of ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0, with a≠0a \neq 0a=0.

Use it when: a quadratic does not factor easily. It works for every quadratic equation in standard form.

Example: For 2x2−3x−2=02x^2 - 3x - 2 = 02x2−3x−2=0, x=3±9+164=3±54x = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 16}}{4} = \frac{3 \pm 5}{4}x=43±9+16​​=43±5​, so x=2x = 2x=2 or x=−12x = -\tfrac{1}{2}x=−21​.

2. Discriminant

Δ=b2−4ac\Delta = b^2 - 4acΔ=b2−4ac

Symbols: Δ\DeltaΔ is the expression under the square root in the quadratic formula.

Use it when: you need to know what kind of roots a quadratic has without solving it. Δ>0\Delta > 0Δ>0 gives two real roots, Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 one repeated real root, and Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 two complex roots.

Example: For x2+4x+5=0x^2 + 4x + 5 = 0x2+4x+5=0, Δ=16−20=−4\Delta = 16 - 20 = -4Δ=16−20=−4, so there are no real solutions.

3. Square of a sum or difference

(a±b)2=a2±2ab+b2(a \pm b)^2 = a^2 \pm 2ab + b^2(a±b)2=a2±2ab+b2

Symbols: aaa and bbb are any real numbers or expressions.

Use it when: you expand a squared binomial, complete the square, or do mental arithmetic.

Example: 1032=(100+3)2=10000+600+9=10609103^2 = (100 + 3)^2 = 10000 + 600 + 9 = 106091032=(100+3)2=10000+600+9=10609.

4. Difference of squares

a2−b2=(a+b)(a−b)a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)a2−b2=(a+b)(a−b)

Symbols: aaa and bbb are any real numbers or expressions.

Use it when: you factor an expression made of two perfect squares separated by a minus sign, or multiply two numbers placed evenly around a round number.

Example: 52×48=(50+2)(50−2)=2500−4=249652 \times 48 = (50 + 2)(50 - 2) = 2500 - 4 = 249652×48=(50+2)(50−2)=2500−4=2496.

5. Sum and difference of cubes

a3+b3=(a+b)(a2−ab+b2),a3−b3=(a−b)(a2+ab+b2)a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2), \qquad a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)a3+b3=(a+b)(a2−ab+b2),a3−b3=(a−b)(a2+ab+b2)

Symbols: aaa and bbb are any real numbers or expressions.

Use it when: you factor a sum or difference of two cubes. The quadratic factor does not factor further over the real numbers.

Example: x3−8=(x−2)(x2+2x+4)x^3 - 8 = (x - 2)(x^2 + 2x + 4)x3−8=(x−2)(x2+2x+4). Check at x=3x = 3x=3: 27−8=1927 - 8 = 1927−8=19 and (1)(9+6+4)=19(1)(9 + 6 + 4) = 19(1)(9+6+4)=19.

6. Binomial theorem

(x+y)n=∑k=0n(nk)xn−kyk(x + y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^{n-k} y^{k}(x+y)n=k=0∑n​(kn​)xn−kyk

Symbols: nnn is a non-negative integer and (nk)=n!k!(n−k)!\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}(kn​)=k!(n−k)!n!​ is a binomial coefficient.

Use it when: you expand a power of a binomial, or need one specific term without expanding everything.

Example: (x+2)4=x4+8x3+24x2+32x+16(x + 2)^4 = x^4 + 8x^3 + 24x^2 + 32x + 16(x+2)4=x4+8x3+24x2+32x+16, using the coefficients (4k)2k=1,8,24,32,16\binom{4}{k} 2^k = 1, 8, 24, 32, 16(k4​)2k=1,8,24,32,16.

7. Vertex of a parabola

86. Conditional probability

P(A∣B)=P(A∩B)P(B),P(B)>0P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B) > 0P(A∣B)=P(B)P(A∩B)​,P(B)>0

Symbols: P(A∣B)P(A \mid B)P(A∣B) is the probability of AAA given that BBB has happened.

Use it when: new information shrinks the sample space.

Example: Given that a drawn card is a face card, the chance it is a king is 4/5212/52=13\frac{4/52}{12/52} = \frac{1}{3}12/524/52​=31​.

87. Multiplication rule for independent events

P(A∩B)=P(A) P(B)P(A \cap B) = P(A)\, P(B)P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)

Symbols: AAA and BBB are independent: knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other.

Use it when: you combine separate experiments, such as a coin flip and a die roll.

Example: Heads and a six: 12⋅16=112\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}21​⋅61​=121​.

88. Permutations

P(n,r)=n!(n−r)!P(n, r) = \frac{n!}{(n - r)!}P(n,r)=(n−r)!n!​

Symbols: nnn distinct objects, rrr of them chosen, order matters; n!=n(n−1)⋯1n! = n(n-1)\cdots 1n!=n(n−1)⋯1.

Use it when: you count arrangements, rankings or codes.

Example: Gold, silver and bronze among 10 runners: P(10,3)=10⋅9⋅8=720P(10, 3) = 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 = 720P(10,3)=10⋅9⋅8=720.

89. Combinations

C(n,r)=(nr)=n!r! (n−r)!C(n, r) = \binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}C(n,r)=(rn​)=r!(n−r)!n!​

Symbols: nnn distinct objects, rrr chosen, order does not matter.

Use it when: you count committees, hands of cards or subsets.

Example: Choosing 3 of 10 people for a committee: C(10,3)=7206=120C(10, 3) = \frac{720}{6} = 120C(10,3)=6720​=120.

90. Mean

xˉ=1n∑i=1nxi\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_ixˉ=n1​i=1∑n​xi​

Symbols: x1,…,xnx_1, \dots, x_nx1​,…,xn​ are the data values and nnn is how many there are. For a whole population the mean is written μ\muμ.

Use it when: you summarize the center of numerical data.

Example: For 4, 8, 6, 5, 7: xˉ=305=6\bar{x} = \frac{30}{5} = 6xˉ=530​=6.

91. Standard deviation

s=∑(x−xˉ)2n−1,σ=∑(x−μ)2Ns = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{N}}s=n−1∑(x−xˉ)2​​,σ=N∑(x−μ)2​​

Symbols: sss is the sample standard deviation (divide by n−1n - 1n−1); σ\sigmaσ is the population standard deviation (divide by the population size NNN).

Use it when: you measure how spread out the data are around the mean.

Example: For 4, 8, 6, 5, 7 the squared deviations from 6 sum to 4+4+0+1+1=104 + 4 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 104+4+0+1+1=10. As a sample, s=10/4≈1.581s = \sqrt{10/4} \approx 1.581s=10/4​≈1.581; as a whole population, σ=10/5≈1.414\sigma = \sqrt{10/5} \approx 1.414σ=10/5​≈1.414.

92. z-score

z=x−μσz = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}z=σx−μ​

Symbols: xxx is a value, μ\muμ the mean and σ\sigmaσ the standard deviation (use xˉ\bar{x}xˉ and sss for a sample).

Use it when: you compare values from different scales, or count how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean.

Example: A score of 85 on a test with μ=70\mu = 70μ=70 and σ=10\sigma = 10σ=10 has z=1.5z = 1.5z=1.5.

93. Binomial probability

P(X=x)=(nx)pxqn−x,μ=np,σ=npqP(X = x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x q^{n - x}, \qquad \mu = np, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{npq}P(X=x)=(xn​)pxqn−x,μ=np,σ=npq​

Symbols: nnn independent trials, each a success with probability ppp; q=1−pq = 1 - pq=1−p; XXX counts the successes.

Use it when: you count successes in a fixed number of independent yes/no trials with the same probability.

Example: Exactly 3 heads in 5 fair flips: (53)(0.5)5=1032=0.3125\binom{5}{3}(0.5)^5 = \frac{10}{32} = 0.3125(35​)(0.5)5=3210​=0.3125. Here μ=2.5\mu = 2.5μ=2.5 and σ=1.25≈1.118\sigma = \sqrt{1.25} \approx 1.118σ=1.25​≈1.118.

Vectors and matrices

Vector formulas follow OpenStax Calculus Volume 3, sections 2.2 to 2.4; matrix formulas follow Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, sections 11.7 and 11.8.

94. Magnitude of a vector

∥v∥=v12+v22+v32\lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}∥v∥=v12​+v22​+v32​​

Symbols: v=⟨v1,v2,v3⟩\mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \ranglev=⟨v1​,v2​,v3​⟩. The unit vector in the same direction is v∥v∥\frac{\mathbf{v}}{\lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert}∥v∥v​ for v≠0\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}v=0.

Use it when: you need the length of a vector, such as a speed from a velocity vector.

Example: ∥⟨2,3,6⟩∥=4+9+36=7\lVert \langle 2, 3, 6 \rangle \rVert = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = 7∥⟨2,3,6⟩∥=4+9+36​=7, so the unit vector is ⟨27,37,67⟩\langle \tfrac{2}{7}, \tfrac{3}{7}, \tfrac{6}{7} \rangle⟨72​,73​,76​⟩.

95. Dot product

u⋅v=u1v1+u2v2+u3v3\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3u⋅v=u1​v1​+u2​v2​+u3​v3​

Symbols: u\mathbf{u}u and v\mathbf{v}v are vectors; the result is a scalar.

Use it when: you test perpendicularity (dot product zero), compute work, or find projections.

Example: ⟨1,2,3⟩⋅⟨4,−5,6⟩=4−10+18=12\langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle \cdot \langle 4, -5, 6 \rangle = 4 - 10 + 18 = 12⟨1,2,3⟩⋅⟨4,−5,6⟩=4−10+18=12.

96. Angle between two vectors

cos⁡θ=u⋅v∥u∥ ∥v∥\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert}cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​

Symbols: θ\thetaθ is the angle between nonzero vectors u\mathbf{u}u and v\mathbf{v}v, with 0≤θ≤π0 \leq \theta \leq \pi0≤θ≤π.

Use it when: you need the angle between two directions, or a similarity measure between vectors.

Example: For ⟨1,0⟩\langle 1, 0 \rangle⟨1,0⟩ and ⟨1,1⟩\langle 1, 1 \rangle⟨1,1⟩: cos⁡θ=11⋅2\cos\theta = \frac{1}{1 \cdot \sqrt{2}}cosθ=1⋅2​1​, so θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circθ=45∘.

97. Cross product

u×v=⟨u2v3−u3v2,  u3v1−u1v3,  u1v2−u2v1⟩,∥u×v∥=∥u∥ ∥v∥sin⁡θ\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \langle u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2,\; u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3,\; u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1 \rangle, \qquad \lVert \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} \rVert = \lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert \sin\thetau×v=⟨u2​v3​−u3​v2​,u3​v1​−u1​v3​,u1​v2​−u2​v1​⟩,∥u×v∥=∥u∥∥v∥sinθ

Symbols: u\mathbf{u}u and v\mathbf{v}v are 3D vectors; the result is perpendicular to both, and its length is the area of the parallelogram they span.

Use it when: you need a normal vector to a plane, a torque, or the area of a parallelogram or triangle in 3D.

Example: ⟨1,2,3⟩×⟨4,5,6⟩=⟨−3,6,−3⟩\langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle \times \langle 4, 5, 6 \rangle = \langle -3, 6, -3 \rangle⟨1,2,3⟩×⟨4,5,6⟩=⟨−3,6,−3⟩, so the parallelogram has area 54≈7.348\sqrt{54} \approx 7.34854​≈7.348.

98. Determinant of a 2×2 matrix

det⁡(abcd)=ad−bc\det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bcdet(ac​bd​)=ad−bc

Symbols: aaa, bbb, ccc and ddd are the matrix entries.

Use it when: you check whether a matrix is invertible (nonzero determinant), solve systems with Cramer's rule, or find an area scale factor.

Example: det⁡(3846)=18−32=−14\det\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 8 \\ 4 & 6 \end{pmatrix} = 18 - 32 = -14det(34​86​)=18−32=−14.

99. Inverse of a 2×2 matrix

A−1=1ad−bc(d−b−ca),ad−bc≠0A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}, \qquad ad - bc \neq 0A−1=ad−bc1​(d−c​−ba​),ad−bc=0

Symbols: A=(abcd)A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}A=(ac​bd​). Swap aaa and ddd, negate bbb and ccc, and divide by the determinant.

Use it when: you solve AX=BAX = BAX=B as X=A−1BX = A^{-1}BX=A−1B, or undo a linear transformation.

Example: For A=(4726)A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 2 & 6 \end{pmatrix}A=(42​76​), det⁡A=10\det A = 10detA=10 and A−1=(0.6−0.7−0.20.4)A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 & -0.7 \\ -0.2 & 0.4 \end{pmatrix}A−1=(0.6−0.2​−0.70.4​).

100. Cramer's rule for a 2×2 system

x=DxD,y=DyD,D=∣a1b1a2b2∣≠0x = \frac{D_x}{D}, \qquad y = \frac{D_y}{D}, \qquad D = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & b_1 \\ a_2 & b_2 \end{vmatrix} \neq 0x=DDx​​,y=DDy​​,D=​a1​a2​​b1​b2​​​=0

Symbols: The system is a1x+b1y=c1a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1a1​x+b1​y=c1​ and a2x+b2y=c2a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2a2​x+b2​y=c2​. DxD_xDx​ replaces the xxx-column of DDD with c1,c2c_1, c_2c1​,c2​; DyD_yDy​ replaces the yyy-column.

Use it when: you solve a small linear system and the determinant is nonzero.

Example: For 2x+3y=82x + 3y = 82x+3y=8 and x−y=−1x - y = -1x−y=−1: D=−5D = -5D=−5, Dx=−5D_x = -5Dx​=−5, Dy=−10D_y = -10Dy​=−10, so x=1x = 1x=1 and y=2y = 2y=2.

Common mistakes

These are the slips that most often turn a correct formula into a wrong answer. Each one can be caught by checking the conditions listed with the formula above.

  • Squaring a sum term by term. (a+b)2≠a2+b2(a + b)^2 \neq a^2 + b^2(a+b)2=a2+b2; the 2ab2ab2ab term is missing. With a=3a = 3a=3 and b=4b = 4b=4, (a+b)2=49(a + b)^2 = 49(a+b)2=49 but a2+b2=25a^2 + b^2 = 25a2+b2=25. Similarly, a2+b2≠a+b\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} \neq a + ba2+b2​=a+b.
  • Inventing log rules. log⁡(M+N)\log(M + N)log(M+N) does not split into log⁡M+log⁡N\log M + \log NlogM+logN. The product rule is about log⁡(MN)\log(MN)log(MN).
  • Using degrees where radians are required. Arc length, sector area, lim⁡θ→0sin⁡θθ=1\lim_{\theta \to 0} \frac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1limθ→0​θsinθ​=1 and every trigonometric derivative and integral assume radians. In degrees the same limit is π180≈0.01745\frac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745180π​≈0.01745, not 1.
  • Dropping the inner derivative. In the chain rule, ddxsin⁡(3x)=3cos⁡(3x)\frac{d}{dx}\sin(3x) = 3\cos(3x)dxd​sin(3x)=3cos(3x), not cos⁡(3x)\cos(3x)cos(3x).
  • Reversing the quotient rule numerator. It is f′g−fg′f'g - fg'f′g−fg′; swapping the order flips the sign of the answer.
  • Forgetting the constant of integration. Every indefinite integral needs +C+ C+C.
  • Summing an infinite geometric series that diverges. a11−r\frac{a_1}{1 - r}1−ra1​​ only applies when −1<r<1-1 < r < 1−1<r<1. For 1+2+4+⋯1 + 2 + 4 + \cdots1+2+4+⋯ it would give −1-1−1, which is meaningless.
  • Multiplying probabilities of dependent events. P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) only holds for independent events; otherwise use P(A∩B)=P(A∣B)P(B)P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B)P(A∩B)=P(A∣B)P(B).
  • Mixing up permutations and combinations. If swapping two chosen items gives a new outcome, order matters and you need permutations.
  • Choosing the wrong standard deviation. Divide by n−1n - 1n−1 for a sample and by NNN for a full population.
  • Taking only the negative of a slope for a perpendicular line. The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: 222 becomes −12-\frac{1}{2}−21​, not −2-2−2.
  • Ignoring the sign in half-angle formulas. Choose +++ or −-− from the quadrant of α2\frac{\alpha}{2}2α​, not of α\alphaα.

Next steps

A list of formulas is only useful once you can pick the right one quickly. To build that skill:

  • Practise faster mental shortcuts in math tricks to solve problems faster.
  • Apply items 1 to 9 to full problems in algebra problems with solutions for beginners.
  • See items 83 to 93 used on real data in probability and statistics real-world examples.
  • Take items 94 to 100 further in linear algebra concepts for machine learning.
  • Browse more articles and blogs in the mathematics category.

References

  • Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, Jay Abramson, OpenStax (2021). https://openstax.org/books/algebra-and-trigonometry-2e/pages/2-5-quadratic-equations
  • Prealgebra 2e, Lynn Marecek, MaryAnne Anthony-Smith and Andrea Honeycutt Mathis, OpenStax (2020). https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/9-6-solve-geometry-applications-volume-and-surface-area
  • Intermediate Algebra 2e, Lynn Marecek and Andrea Honeycutt Mathis, OpenStax (2020). https://openstax.org/books/intermediate-algebra-2e/pages/11-1-distance-and-midpoint-formulas-circles
  • Calculus Volume 1, Gilbert Strang and Edwin "Jed" Herman, OpenStax (2016). https://openstax.org/books/calculus-volume-1/pages/3-3-differentiation-rules
  • Calculus Volume 2, Gilbert Strang and Edwin "Jed" Herman, OpenStax (2016). https://openstax.org/books/calculus-volume-2/pages/3-1-integration-by-parts
  • Calculus Volume 3, Gilbert Strang and Edwin "Jed" Herman, OpenStax (2016). https://openstax.org/books/calculus-volume-3/pages/2-3-the-dot-product
  • Introductory Statistics 2e, Barbara Illowsky and Susan Dean, OpenStax (2023). https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/2-7-measures-of-the-spread-of-the-data

title: 101 Best Math Tricks to Solve Problems Faster
description: 101 math tricks for mental multiplication, squares, divisibility, percents, algebra and geometry, each with a proof, a worked example and its limits.
author: BlogAI Editors
html:
Most "math tricks" are not tricks at all. They are ordinary algebra applied to numbers with a convenient shape: a number close to 100, a number ending in 5, a divisor that happens to split 1000 or 1001. Once you see the algebra, the shortcut stops being something to memorize and becomes something you can rebuild on the spot, and you also learn exactly when it breaks.

That is the approach of this list. Every one of the 101 tricks below comes with four parts:

  • The trick: what to do.
  • Why it works: a short algebraic justification.
  • Example: a worked calculation. Every example and identity in this article was checked with a computer algebra script before publication.
  • When it does not apply: the limits, so you do not use a shortcut outside its range.

A fair warning before you start. In a long-running Physics Forums discussion about "human calculator" techniques, posters pointed out that many tricks only cover specific number patterns and that the real bottleneck is holding intermediate digits in your head, which improves only with practice (Physics Forums, 2016). That matches the design of this list: learn the handful that fit the problems you actually meet, and treat the rest as worked examples of why algebra is useful.

The final section turns from arithmetic to strategy. George Pólya's How to Solve It (Princeton University Press, first published 1945) describes problem solving in four phases (understand the problem, devise a plan, carry it out, look back) and collects heuristics such as working backwards, drawing a figure and solving a simpler related problem (Princeton University Press; Wikipedia summary). Those heuristics often save more time than any arithmetic shortcut.

Mental multiplication tricks

1. Multiply by 5: multiply by 10, then halve

The trick. To compute 5×n5 \times n5×n, compute 10×n10 \times n10×n and divide by 2.

Why it works. 5=1025 = \dfrac{10}{2}5=210​, so 5n=10n25n = \dfrac{10n}{2}5n=210n​.

Example. 5×68=680÷2=3405 \times 68 = 680 \div 2 = 3405×68=680÷2=340, and 5×47=470÷2=2355 \times 47 = 470 \div 2 = 2355×47=470÷2=235.

When it does not apply. It always works, but it is only faster when halving is easy. Halving 10n10n10n is usually easier than halving nnn first, because 10n10n10n is always even.

2. Multiply by 25: multiply by 100, then divide by 4

The trick. 25×n=100n÷425 \times n = 100n \div 425×n=100n÷4.

Why it works. 25=100425 = \dfrac{100}{4}25=4100​.

Example. 25×36=3600÷4=90025 \times 36 = 3600 \div 4 = 90025×36=3600÷4=900. Alternatively, divide first: 36÷4=936 \div 4 = 936÷4=9, so the answer is 900900900.

When it does not apply. Dividing first is only clean when nnn is a multiple of 4. Otherwise divide 100n100n100n by 4, or split: 25×38=25×36+25×2=95025 \times 38 = 25 \times 36 + 25 \times 2 = 95025×38=25×36+25×2=950.

3. Multiply by 9: multiply by 10, then subtract once

The trick. 9×n=10n−n9 \times n = 10n - n9×n=10n−n.

Why it works. 9=10−19 = 10 - 19=10−1, and multiplication distributes over subtraction.

Example. 9×47=470−47=4239 \times 47 = 470 - 47 = 4239×47=470−47=423.

When it does not apply. It always holds. The only risk is a borrowing error in the subtraction, so check the last digit: 9×7=639 \times 7 = 639×7=63 ends in 3, and so does 423.

4. Multiply a two-digit number by 11: put the digit sum in the middle

The trick. For a two-digit number with digits aaa and bbb, write aaa, then a+ba + ba+b, then bbb. If a+b≥10a + b \ge 10a+b≥10, carry the 1 into the hundreds.

Why it works.

11(10a+b)=110a+11b=100a+10(a+b)+b11(10a + b) = 110a + 11b = 100a + 10(a + b) + b11(10a+b)=110a+11b=100a+10(a+b)+b

Example. 11×4311 \times 4311×43: 444, 4+3=74 + 3 = 74+3=7, 333 gives 473473473. With a carry, 11×8711 \times 8711×87: 888, 151515, 777 becomes 957957957.

When it does not apply. For longer numbers you must add each neighbouring pair of digits (for example 11×352=387211 \times 352 = 387211×352=3872), and carries can chain, so the trick loses its speed advantage.

5. Multiply by 99: multiply by 100, then subtract once

The trick. 99×n=100n−n99 \times n = 100n - n99×n=100n−n.

Why it works. 99=100−199 = 100 - 199=100−1.

Example. 99×34=3400−34=336699 \times 34 = 3400 - 34 = 336699×34=3400−34=3366.

When it does not apply. Always valid. The same idea gives 999×n=1000n−n999 \times n = 1000n - n999×n=1000n−n, but the subtraction gets harder for large nnn.

6. Multiply a two-digit number by 101: write it twice

The trick. For a two-digit number nnn, 101×n101 \times n101×n is nnn written twice.

Why it works. 101n=100n+n101n = 100n + n101n=100n+n. Shifting a two-digit nnn two places left leaves exactly two empty places for the second copy.

Example. 101×47=4747101 \times 47 = 4747101×47=4747.

When it does not apply. For three-digit numbers the copies overlap: 101×347=34700+347=35047101 \times 347 = 34700 + 347 = 35047101×347=34700+347=35047, not 347347347347347347. (Writing a three-digit number twice is multiplication by 100110011001.)

7. Double one factor and halve the other

The trick. If one factor is even, halve it and double the other. Repeat until the product is easy.

Why it works. a×b=a2×2ba \times b = \dfrac{a}{2} \times 2ba×b=2a​×2b, because 12×2=1\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 = 121​×2=1.

Example. 16×35=8×70=56016 \times 35 = 8 \times 70 = 56016×35=8×70=560.

When it does not apply. Halving an odd number produces a fraction, so stop when neither factor halves cleanly. The trick also does not help when neither number becomes "round".

8. Split one factor into tens and units

The trick. Break one factor into parts that are easy to multiply, then add the partial products.

Why it works. The distributive property: a(b+c)=ab+aca(b + c) = ab + aca(b+c)=ab+ac.

Example. 7×68=7×60+7×8=420+56=4767 \times 68 = 7 \times 60 + 7 \times 8 = 420 + 56 = 4767×68=7×60+7×8=420+56=476.

When it does not apply. Always valid. When both factors have several digits, the number of partial products grows quickly, and other tricks in this section are faster.

9. Round, multiply, then compensate

The trick. Round a factor to a nearby round number, multiply, then subtract (or add) the overshoot.

Why it works. a(b−k)=ab−aka(b - k) = ab - aka(b−k)=ab−ak.

Example. 6×49=6×50−6=2946 \times 49 = 6 \times 50 - 6 = 2946×49=6×50−6=294, and 7×198=7×200−7×2=13867 \times 198 = 7 \times 200 - 7 \times 2 = 13867×198=7×200−7×2=1386.

When it does not apply. It is only worth it when the rounding distance kkk is small. Remember to multiply the correction by the other factor: 7×1987 \times 1987×198 is 1400−141400 - 141400−14, not 1400−21400 - 21400−2.

10. Multiply two numbers just below 100

The trick. Find each number's deficit from 100. Subtract one deficit from the other number to get the first two digits; multiply the deficits to get the last two.

Why it works.

(100−a)(100−b)=100 (100−a−b)+ab(100 - a)(100 - b) = 100\,(100 - a - b) + ab(100−a)(100−b)=100(100−a−b)+ab

Example. 97×9697 \times 9697×96: deficits 333 and 444. Left part 96−3=9396 - 3 = 9396−3=93, right part 3×4=123 \times 4 = 123×4=12, so 931293129312. With a carry, 88×8988 \times 8988×89: deficits 121212 and 111111, left part 777777, right part 132132132, so 7700+132=78327700 + 132 = 78327700+132=7832.

When it does not apply. If ab≥100ab \ge 100ab≥100, the right part spills into the hundreds and must be added, not written beside the left part. The trick is slow for numbers far from 100.

11. Multiply two numbers just above 100

The trick. Add one number's excess over 100 to the other number for the leading digits; multiply the excesses for the last two digits.

Why it works.

(100+a)(100+b)=100 (100+a+b)+ab(100 + a)(100 + b) = 100\,(100 + a + b) + ab(100+a)(100+b)=100(100+a+b)+ab

Example. 104×107104 \times 107104×107: 107+4=111107 + 4 = 111107+4=111, 4×7=284 \times 7 = 284×7=28, so 111281112811128.

When it does not apply. Same carry rule as trick 10 when ab≥100ab \ge 100ab≥100. If one number is above 100 and one below, the product ababab is negative and must be subtracted: 103×98=100×101−6=10094103 \times 98 = 100 \times 101 - 6 = 10094103×98=100×101−6=10094.

12. Same tens digit, units that add to 10

The trick. If two two-digit numbers share a tens digit aaa and their units digits add to 10, multiply aaa by a+1a + 1a+1, then append the product of the units digits as two digits.

Why it works. With units bbb and ccc where b+c=10b + c = 10b+c=10:

(10a+b)(10a+c)=100a2+10a(b+c)+bc=100 a(a+1)+bc(10a + b)(10a + c) = 100a^2 + 10a(b + c) + bc = 100\,a(a + 1) + bc(10a+b)(10a+c)=100a2+10a(b+c)+bc=100a(a+1)+bc

Example. 43×4743 \times 4743×47: 4×5=204 \times 5 = 204×5=20, 3×7=213 \times 7 = 213×7=21, so 202120212021. And 62×68=421662 \times 68 = 421662×68=4216.

When it does not apply. Both conditions are required. 43×4843 \times 4843×48 fails because 3+8≠103 + 8 \ne 103+8=10. Write bcbcbc with two digits: 41×49=200941 \times 49 = 200941×49=2009, not 209209209.

13. Use the midpoint: difference of squares

The trick. If two numbers are equally spaced around an easy number mmm, the product is m2m^2m2 minus the square of the gap.

Why it works. (m−d)(m+d)=m2−d2(m - d)(m + d) = m^2 - d^2(m−d)(m+d)=m2−d2, the difference-of-squares identity (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §1.4).

Example. 47×53=502−32=2500−9=249147 \times 53 = 50^2 - 3^2 = 2500 - 9 = 249147×53=502−32=2500−9=2491, and 38×42=1600−4=159638 \times 42 = 1600 - 4 = 159638×42=1600−4=1596.

When it does not apply. The numbers must be the same distance from an easy square, which means their sum must be even. For 47×5447 \times 5447×54, use 47×53+47=253847 \times 53 + 47 = 253847×53+47=2538.

14. Multiply two "teens"

The trick. For 13×1713 \times 1713×17: add one number to the units digit of the other (13+7=2013 + 7 = 2013+7=20), multiply by 10, then add the product of the units digits (3×7=213 \times 7 = 213×7=21).

Why it works.

(10+a)(10+b)=10 (10+a+b)+ab(10 + a)(10 + b) = 10\,(10 + a + b) + ab(10+a)(10+b)=10(10+a+b)+ab

Example. 13×17=200+21=22113 \times 17 = 200 + 21 = 22113×17=200+21=221, and 16×18=240+48=28816 \times 18 = 240 + 48 = 28816×18=240+48=288.

When it does not apply. Only for numbers from 11 to 19. The same idea works around any base, such as 20 or 50, if you replace the 10s with that base.

15. Factor into friendly pairs

The trick. Break factors apart to create pairs such as 4×25=1004 \times 25 = 1004×25=100 or 8×125=10008 \times 125 = 10008×125=1000.

Why it works. Multiplication is associative and commutative, so factors can be regrouped freely.

Example. 32×125=4×(8×125)=4×1000=400032 \times 125 = 4 \times (8 \times 125) = 4 \times 1000 = 400032×125=4×(8×125)=4×1000=4000, and 44×25=11×(4×25)=110044 \times 25 = 11 \times (4 \times 25) = 110044×25=11×(4×25)=1100.

When it does not apply. Only when the factors contain the right partners. 33×12533 \times 12533×125 has no factor of 8, so use trick 9 instead (32×125+12532 \times 125 + 12532×125+125).

16. Cross-multiply two-digit numbers

The trick. For ab‾×cd‾\overline{ab} \times \overline{cd}ab×cd, compute three columns from right to left: b×db \times db×d, then a×d+b×ca \times d + b \times ca×d+b×c, then a×ca \times ca×c, carrying as you go.

Why it works.

(10a+b)(10c+d)=100 ac+10 (ad+bc)+bd(10a + b)(10c + d) = 100\,ac + 10\,(ad + bc) + bd(10a+b)(10c+d)=100ac+10(ad+bc)+bd

Example. 23×4123 \times 4123×41: 3×1=33 \times 1 = 33×1=3; 2×1+3×4=142 \times 1 + 3 \times 4 = 142×1+3×4=14, write 4 carry 1; 2×4+1=92 \times 4 + 1 = 92×4+1=9. Answer 943943943. For 67×5867 \times 5867×58: 565656 (write 6, carry 5); 6×8+7×5+5=886 \times 8 + 7 \times 5 + 5 = 886×8+7×5+5=88 (write 8, carry 8); 6×5+8=386 \times 5 + 8 = 386×5+8=38. Answer 388638863886.

When it does not apply. It always works, but it demands holding carries in memory. If a number is near 100 or near a round number, tricks 9 to 13 are easier.

Squares and roots

17. Square a number ending in 5

The trick. For a number written as "$a$5", multiply aaa by a+1a + 1a+1 and append 25.

Why it works.

(10a+5)2=100a2+100a+25=100 a(a+1)+25(10a + 5)^2 = 100a^2 + 100a + 25 = 100\,a(a + 1) + 25(10a+5)2=100a2+100a+25=100a(a+1)+25

Example. 65265^2652: 6×7=426 \times 7 = 426×7=42, so 422542254225. 1152115^21152: 11×12=13211 \times 12 = 13211×12=132, so 132251322513225.

When it does not apply. Only for numbers ending in 5. For a product like 65×7565 \times 7565×75, use trick 13 (702−52=487570^2 - 5^2 = 4875702−52=4875).

18. Square a number near 50

The trick. For 50+d50 + d50+d, add ddd to 25 for the first two digits and append d2d^2d2 as two digits.

Why it works.

(50+d)2=2500+100d+d2=100 (25+d)+d2(50 + d)^2 = 2500 + 100d + d^2 = 100\,(25 + d) + d^2(50+d)2=2500+100d+d2=100(25+d)+d2

Example. 53253^2532: 25+3=2825 + 3 = 2825+3=28, 32=093^2 = 0932=09, so 280928092809. 47247^2472: 25−3=2225 - 3 = 2225−3=22, 090909, so 220922092209.

When it does not apply. d2d^2d2 must fit in two digits, so it is clean only for ∣d∣≤9|d| \le 9∣d∣≤9, that is, from 41 to 59.

19. Square a number near 100

The trick. For 100+d100 + d100+d, the first part is 100+2d100 + 2d100+2d and the last two digits are d2d^2d2.

Why it works. (100+d)2=100 (100+2d)+d2(100 + d)^2 = 100\,(100 + 2d) + d^2(100+d)2=100(100+2d)+d2, which is the perfect-square pattern (a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2 (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §1.4).

Example. 97297^2972: 100−6=94100 - 6 = 94100−6=94, 32=093^2 = 0932=09, so 940994099409. 1042104^21042: 108108108, 161616, so 108161081610816.

When it does not apply. Again d2d^2d2 must stay below 100, so it is clean for ∣d∣≤9|d| \le 9∣d∣≤9.

20. Step from a square you know

The trick. To get (n+1)2(n + 1)^2(n+1)2 from n2n^2n2, add nnn and n+1n + 1n+1.

Why it works. (n+1)2−n2=2n+1=n+(n+1)(n + 1)^2 - n^2 = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1)(n+1)2−n2=2n+1=n+(n+1).

Example. 312=302+30+31=96131^2 = 30^2 + 30 + 31 = 961312=302+30+31=961, and 412=1600+40+41=168141^2 = 1600 + 40 + 41 = 1681412=1600+40+41=1681.

When it does not apply. It works for neighbours. For larger steps use (n+k)2=n2+2nk+k2(n + k)^2 = n^2 + 2nk + k^2(n+k)2=n2+2nk+k2, and do not drop the 2nk2nk2nk term.

21. Square by moving to a round number

The trick. To square nnn, move down by ddd and up by ddd to make one factor round, multiply, then add d2d^2d2.

Why it works. n2=(n−d)(n+d)+d2n^2 = (n - d)(n + d) + d^2n2=(n−d)(n+d)+d2.

Example. 482=46×50+22=2300+4=230448^2 = 46 \times 50 + 2^2 = 2300 + 4 = 2304482=46×50+22=2300+4=2304, and 872=84×90+9=756987^2 = 84 \times 90 + 9 = 7569872=84×90+9=7569.

When it does not apply. Always valid, but only helpful when the new product is easy. Forgetting +d2+d^2+d2 is the usual mistake.

22. Sums of consecutive odd numbers are squares

The trick. The sum of the first nnn odd numbers is n2n^2n2.

Why it works. ∑k=1n(2k−1)=2⋅n(n+1)2−n=n2\sum_{k=1}^{n} (2k - 1) = 2 \cdot \dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2} - n = n^2∑k=1n​(2k−1)=2⋅2n(n+1)​−n=n2.

Example. 1+3+5+⋯+191 + 3 + 5 + \dots + 191+3+5+⋯+19 has 10 terms, so the sum is 102=10010^2 = 100102=100.

When it does not apply. The sum must start at 1 and skip no odd numbers. For 11+13+⋯+1911 + 13 + \dots + 1911+13+⋯+19, compute 102−52=7510^2 - 5^2 = 75102−52=75.

23. Rule out squares by the last digit

The trick. A perfect square can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A whole number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is not a perfect square.

Why it works. The last digit of n2n^2n2 depends only on the last digit of nnn, and the squares 02,12,…,920^2, 1^2, \dots, 9^202,12,…,92 end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1.

Example. 1,234,5671{,}234{,}5671,234,567 ends in 7, so it is not a perfect square.

When it does not apply. The test can only rule numbers out. 5,5555{,}5555,555 ends in 5 and is still not a square.

24. Rule out squares by the digit sum

The trick. Reduce a number by repeatedly adding its digits (its digital root). A perfect square has digital root 1, 4, 7 or 9.

Why it works. A number leaves the same remainder mod 9 as its digit sum (see trick 41), and squares mod 9 can only be 0, 1, 4 or 7.

Example. 5,5555{,}5555,555: 5+5+5+5=205 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 205+5+5+5=20, 2+0=22 + 0 = 22+0=2. Not 1, 4, 7 or 9, so 5,5555{,}5555,555 is not a square. (It sits between 742=547674^2 = 5476742=5476 and 752=562575^2 = 5625752=5625.)

When it does not apply. Like trick 23, it only rules numbers out. 1,234,5671{,}234{,}5671,234,567 has digital root 1 but is not a square.

25. Bracket a square root between two squares

The trick. Find the perfect squares on either side of the number.

Why it works. The square root function is increasing, so a2<x<b2a^2 < x < b^2a2<x<b2 implies a<x<ba < \sqrt{x} < ba<x​<b for positive numbers.

Example. 49<50<6449 < 50 < 6449<50<64, so 7<50<87 < \sqrt{50} < 87<50​<8. And 196<200<225196 < 200 < 225196<200<225 gives 14<200<1514 < \sqrt{200} < 1514<200​<15.

When it does not apply. This gives bounds, not a decimal answer. Use trick 26 to refine it.

26. Refine a square root with one division

The trick. If x=n2+rx = n^2 + rx=n2+r with n2n^2n2 the nearest perfect square, then x≈n+r2n\sqrt{x} \approx n + \dfrac{r}{2n}x​≈n+2nr​.

Why it works. (n+r2n)2=n2+r+r24n2\left(n + \dfrac{r}{2n}\right)^2 = n^2 + r + \dfrac{r^2}{4n^2}(n+2nr​)2=n2+r+4n2r2​, which differs from xxx only by the small term r24n2\dfrac{r^2}{4n^2}4n2r2​.

Example. 50≈7+114≈7.0714\sqrt{50} \approx 7 + \dfrac{1}{14} \approx 7.071450​≈7+141​≈7.0714; the true value is 7.07117.07117.0711. For 80\sqrt{80}80​, use 818181: 9−118≈8.9449 - \dfrac{1}{18} \approx 8.9449−181​≈8.944.

When it does not apply. The error grows when rrr is large compared with nnn, and the estimate is always slightly too high. Use the nearest square, even if rrr is negative: starting 80\sqrt{80}80​ from 646464 gives 999, a poor estimate.

27. Simplify a radical by pulling out square factors

The trick. Factor out the largest perfect square.

Why it works. a2b=ab\sqrt{a^2 b} = a\sqrt{b}a2b​=ab​ for a,b≥0a, b \ge 0a,b≥0.

Example. 72=36⋅2=62\sqrt{72} = \sqrt{36 \cdot 2} = 6\sqrt{2}72​=36⋅2​=62​.

When it does not apply. The rule splits products, not sums: 9+16=5\sqrt{9 + 16} = 59+16​=5, while 9+16=7\sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16} = 79​+16​=7.

28. Find the square root of a perfect square from its last digit

The trick. Use the last digit to narrow the root's last digit to two options, bracket the root between multiples of 10, then test the midpoint ending in 5.

Why it works. By trick 23's table, a square ending in 6 has a root ending in 4 or 6 (similarly 1 ↔ 1 or 9, 4 ↔ 2 or 8, 9 ↔ 3 or 7). Squares grow with the root, so comparing with (10a+5)2(10a + 5)^2(10a+5)2 picks the lower or upper option.

Example. 5476\sqrt{5476}5476​: ends in 6, so the root ends in 4 or 6. 702=4900<5476<6400=80270^2 = 4900 < 5476 < 6400 = 80^2702=4900<5476<6400=802, so the root is 74 or 76. Since 752=5625>547675^2 = 5625 > 5476752=5625>5476, the root is 747474.

When it does not apply. Only for numbers you already know are perfect squares. Otherwise use tricks 25 and 26.

29. Find the cube root of a perfect cube

The trick. The last digit of a perfect cube identifies the last digit of its root. Then find the tens digit from the part of the number before the last three digits.

Why it works. The cubes 03,13,…,930^3, 1^3, \dots, 9^303,13,…,93 end in 0, 1, 8, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 9, which are all different, so each last digit points to exactly one root digit. Dropping the last three digits divides roughly by 10310^3103, which removes the units digit from the root.

Example. 4052243\sqrt[3]{405224}3405224​: last digit 4 means the root ends in 4. The leading part 405405405 lies between 73=3437^3 = 34373=343 and 83=5128^3 = 51283=512, so the tens digit is 7. Root: 747474. Likewise 8573753=95\sqrt[3]{857375} = 953857375​=95.

When it does not apply. Only for perfect cubes with a two-digit root. A number that is not a perfect cube will still produce an answer, but it will be wrong.

Divisibility rules

30. Divisibility by 2, 5 and 10: look at the last digit

The trick. A whole number is divisible by 2 if it ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8; by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5; by 10 if it ends in 0 (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §2.4).

Why it works. Write n=10q+rn = 10q + rn=10q+r, where rrr is the last digit. Since 10q10q10q is a multiple of 2, 5 and 10, only rrr decides.

Example. 3,7453{,}7453,745 ends in 5: divisible by 5, not by 2 or 10.

When it does not apply. Last-digit tests only work for divisors of 10. For 4 and 8, use more digits (tricks 31 and 32).

31. Divisibility by 4: last two digits

The trick. A number is divisible by 4 exactly when the number formed by its last two digits is (Wolfram MathWorld).

Why it works. n=100q+rn = 100q + rn=100q+r and 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25, so only rrr matters.

Example. 7,3167{,}3167,316: 161616 is divisible by 4, so 7,3167{,}3167,316 is (7316=4×18297316 = 4 \times 18297316=4×1829).

When it does not apply. An even last digit is not enough: 7,3187{,}3187,318 ends in 18, and 181818 is not divisible by 4.

32. Divisibility by 8: last three digits

The trick. Check the number formed by the last three digits.

Why it works. 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125, so n=1000q+rn = 1000q + rn=1000q+r and only rrr matters.

Example. 5,1285{,}1285,128: 128=8×16128 = 8 \times 16128=8×16, so 5,1285{,}1285,128 is divisible by 8 (5128=8×6415128 = 8 \times 6415128=8×641).

When it does not apply. Checking only the last two digits is not enough: 116116116 ends in 16, which is divisible by 8, but 116116116 is not.

33. Divisibility by 25: ends in 00, 25, 50 or 75

The trick. A number is divisible by 25 when its last two digits are 00, 25, 50 or 75.

Why it works. 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25, so only the last two digits matter, and those four are the two-digit multiples of 25.

Example. 3,4753{,}4753,475 ends in 75, so it is divisible by 25 (3475=25×1393475 = 25 \times 1393475=25×139).

When it does not apply. Ending in 5 is not enough: 3,4653{,}4653,465 ends in 65.

34. Divisibility by 3: digit sum

The trick. A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §2.4).

Why it works. 10=9+110 = 9 + 110=9+1, so every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3. A number ∑dk10k\sum d_k 10^k∑dk​10k therefore leaves the same remainder as ∑dk\sum d_k∑dk​.

Example. 4,5874{,}5874,587: 4+5+8+7=244 + 5 + 8 + 7 = 244+5+8+7=24, divisible by 3, so 4587=3×15294587 = 3 \times 15294587=3×1529.

When it does not apply. The digit sum gives the remainder mod 3, not the quotient.

35. Divisibility by 9: digit sum

The trick. A number is divisible by 9 when its digit sum is.

Why it works. Same reason as trick 34: every power of 10 is 1 more than a multiple of 9.

Example. 4,5874{,}5874,587 has digit sum 24, not a multiple of 9, so it is not divisible by 9. 4,5814{,}5814,581 has digit sum 18, so 4581=9×5094581 = 9 \times 5094581=9×509.

When it does not apply. Do not mix this up with 3: a digit sum of 24 passes the 3 test and fails the 9 test.

36. Divisibility by 6, 12, 15 and friends: combine coprime tests

The trick. To test a composite divisor, split it into factors that share no common factor and run both tests. 6=2×36 = 2 \times 36=2×3, 12=4×312 = 4 \times 312=4×3, 15=3×515 = 3 \times 515=3×5, 18=2×918 = 2 \times 918=2×9.

Why it works. If coprime numbers aaa and bbb both divide nnn, then their product ababab divides nnn.

Example. Is 7,3167{,}3167,316 divisible by 12? It passes the 4 test (trick 31), but its digit sum is 17, so it fails the 3 test. Not divisible by 12.

When it does not apply. The factors must be coprime. 121212 is divisible by both 4 and 6 but not by 24, because 4 and 6 share the factor 2.

37. Divisibility by 11: alternating digit sum

The trick. Starting from the units digit, alternately add and subtract digits. The number is divisible by 11 exactly when this alternating sum is (including 0) (Wolfram MathWorld).

Why it works. 10=11−110 = 11 - 110=11−1, so 10k10^k10k leaves remainder (−1)k(-1)^k(−1)k when divided by 11.

Example. 918,082918{,}082918,082: 2−8+0−8+1−9=−222 - 8 + 0 - 8 + 1 - 9 = -222−8+0−8+1−9=−22, a multiple of 11. Indeed 918082=11×83462918082 = 11 \times 83462918082=11×83462.

When it does not apply. Plain digit sums do not work for 11. A negative alternating sum is fine; only divisibility by 11 matters.

38. Divisibility by 7: subtract twice the last digit

The trick. Remove the last digit yyy, leaving xxx. Then 10x+y10x + y10x+y is divisible by 7 exactly when x−2yx - 2yx−2y is. Repeat as needed (Wolfram MathWorld).

Why it works. (10x+y)−10(x−2y)=21y(10x + y) - 10(x - 2y) = 21y(10x+y)−10(x−2y)=21y, a multiple of 7. Since 10 and 7 share no factor, 10x+y10x + y10x+y is a multiple of 7 exactly when x−2yx - 2yx−2y is.

Example. 343343343: 34−2×3=28=4×734 - 2 \times 3 = 28 = 4 \times 734−2×3=28=4×7. Yes. 2,4012{,}4012,401: 240−2=238240 - 2 = 238240−2=238, then 23−16=723 - 16 = 723−16=7. Yes (2401=742401 = 7^42401=74).

When it does not apply. It answers yes or no; the intermediate numbers are not the remainder. For very long numbers, trick 40 is faster.

39. Divisibility by 13: add four times the last digit

The trick. Remove the last digit yyy, leaving xxx. Then 10x+y10x + y10x+y is divisible by 13 exactly when x+4yx + 4yx+4y is.

Why it works. (10x+y)−10(x+4y)=−39y=−3×13y(10x + y) - 10(x + 4y) = -39y = -3 \times 13y(10x+y)−10(x+4y)=−39y=−3×13y, and 10 shares no factor with 13.

Example. 2,1972{,}1972,197: 219+28=247219 + 28 = 247219+28=247, then 24+28=52=4×1324 + 28 = 52 = 4 \times 1324+28=52=4×13. Yes (2197=1332197 = 13^32197=133).

When it does not apply. Like trick 38, the intermediate values are not remainders. For many digits, use trick 40.

40. Divisibility by 7, 11 and 13 at once: three-digit blocks

The trick. Split the number into groups of three digits from the right and take the alternating sum, starting with +++ on the last group. The original number is divisible by 7, 11 or 13 exactly when this sum is.

Why it works. 1001=7×11×131001 = 7 \times 11 \times 131001=7×11×13, so 100010001000 leaves remainder −1-1−1 for each of the three divisors, and the blocks pick up alternating signs (Cut the Knot; John D. Cook, 2020).

Example. 4,894,498,5184{,}894{,}498{,}5184,894,498,518: 518−498+894−4=910=2×5×7×13518 - 498 + 894 - 4 = 910 = 2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 13518−498+894−4=910=2×5×7×13. So the number is divisible by 7 and 13 but not by 11. (This example comes from John D. Cook's post.)

When it does not apply. The signs must alternate. Simply adding the blocks fails: 100110011001 itself would give 1+1=21 + 1 = 21+1=2.

41. Find a remainder mod 9 from the digit sum

The trick. The remainder of n÷9n \div 9n÷9 equals the remainder of its digit sum divided by 9.

Why it works. Every power of 10 leaves remainder 1 mod 9 (trick 35), so nnn and its digit sum differ by a multiple of 9.

Example. 4,5734{,}5734,573: 4+5+7+3=194 + 5 + 7 + 3 = 194+5+7+3=19, 1+9=101 + 9 = 101+9=10, 1+0=11 + 0 = 11+0=1. So 4573=9×508+14573 = 9 \times 508 + 14573=9×508+1.

When it does not apply. A final digital root of 9 means remainder 0, not 9.

42. Check a multiplication by casting out nines

The trick. Reduce each factor and the claimed answer to their remainders mod 9 (digit sums). The product of the factors' remainders must match the answer's remainder.

Why it works. Remainders multiply: if a≡ra \equiv ra≡r and b≡s(mod9)b \equiv s \pmod 9b≡s(mod9), then ab≡rs(mod9)ab \equiv rs \pmod 9ab≡rs(mod9) (Wolfram MathWorld, Casting Out Nines).

Example. Claim: 348×27=9396348 \times 27 = 9396348×27=9396. Remainders: 348→15→6348 \to 15 \to 6348→15→6, 27→027 \to 027→0, so the product's remainder is 000. And 9396→27→09396 \to 27 \to 09396→27→0. The check passes, and in fact the claim is correct.

When it does not apply. A pass is not a proof. Swapped digits (writing 936993699369) or an extra zero (writing 939609396093960) leave the digit sum unchanged and slip through (Wolfram MathWorld).

43. Add a second check: casting out elevens

The trick. Repeat the check with remainders mod 11, using the alternating digit sum from trick 37.

Why it works. Remainders mod 11 also multiply. Swapping two neighbouring digits aaa and bbb changes the alternating sum by ±2(a−b)\pm 2(a - b)±2(a−b), which is a multiple of 11 only when a=ba = ba=b, so adjacent swaps of different digits are caught.

Example. 348→8−4+3=7348 \to 8 - 4 + 3 = 7348→8−4+3=7; 27→7−2=527 \to 7 - 2 = 527→7−2=5; 7×5=35→27 \times 5 = 35 \to 27×5=35→2. And 9396→6−9+3−9=−9→29396 \to 6 - 9 + 3 - 9 = -9 \to 29396→6−9+3−9=−9→2. Pass. The swapped answer 936993699369 gives 9−6+3−9=−3→89 - 6 + 3 - 9 = -3 \to 89−6+3−9=−3→8, so it fails.

When it does not apply. Errors that change the answer by a multiple of 11 still pass. Use it together with casting out nines, not instead of estimation.

44. Check the last digit of a product

The trick. The last digit of a product equals the last digit of the product of the factors' last digits.

Why it works. (10a+b)(10c+d)=10(… )+bd(10a + b)(10c + d) = 10(\dots) + bd(10a+b)(10c+d)=10(…)+bd, so only bdbdbd affects the units place.

Example. 387×46387 \times 46387×46 must end in 2, because 7×6=427 \times 6 = 427×6=42. A claimed answer of 17,80417{,}80417,804 is wrong; the correct product is 17,80217{,}80217,802.

When it does not apply. It only checks one digit. Pair it with an estimate (trick 61) to check the size.

Fractions, decimals and percentages

45. Swap the numbers in a percentage

The trick. x%x\%x% of yyy equals y%y\%y% of xxx. Use whichever is easier.

Why it works. x100⋅y=y100⋅x\dfrac{x}{100} \cdot y = \dfrac{y}{100} \cdot x100x​⋅y=100y​⋅x, because multiplication is commutative.

Example. 8%8\%8% of 505050 = 50%50\%50% of 888 = 444.

When it does not apply. It only helps when the swapped percentage is friendly, such as 10%, 25% or 50%.

46. Build any percentage from 10%, 5% and 1%

The trick. Find 10% by dividing by 10, halve it for 5%, divide by 10 again for 1%, then combine.

Why it works. A percent is a ratio with denominator 100 (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §6.1), so percentages of the same amount add: 35%=3×10%+5%35\% = 3 \times 10\% + 5\%35%=3×10%+5%.

Example. 35%35\%35% of 240240240: 10%=2410\% = 2410%=24, so 3×24+12=843 \times 24 + 12 = 843×24+12=84.

When it does not apply. "Cross out the last digit" for 10% only works for whole numbers ending in 0. For 10% of 245, move the decimal point: 24.524.524.5. Teachers report this shortcut as a common source of errors (Mr Barton Maths).

47. Change by a percentage with a single multiplier

The trick. To increase by p%p\%p%, multiply by 1+p1001 + \dfrac{p}{100}1+100p​. To decrease by p%p\%p%, multiply by 1−p1001 - \dfrac{p}{100}1−100p​. Convert the percentage to a decimal by moving the decimal point two places left (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §6.1).

Why it works. x+p100x=x(1+p100)x + \dfrac{p}{100}x = x\left(1 + \dfrac{p}{100}\right)x+100p​x=x(1+100p​).

Example. Increase 80 by 30%: 80×1.3=10480 \times 1.3 = 10480×1.3=104. Decrease 60 by 15%: 60×0.85=5160 \times 0.85 = 5160×0.85=51.

When it does not apply. Multiplying by 0.30.30.3 gives the 30% amount (24), not the new total. A multiplier above 1 always increases, so ×1.15\times 1.15×1.15 cannot be a 15% decrease.

48. Chain percentage changes by multiplying

The trick. Successive changes multiply; they do not add.

Why it works. A change of aaa then bbb (as decimals) gives (1+a)(1+b)=1+a+b+ab(1 + a)(1 + b) = 1 + a + b + ab(1+a)(1+b)=1+a+b+ab. The extra ababab is why adding fails.

Example. +20%+20\%+20% then −20%-20\%−20%: 1.2×0.8=0.961.2 \times 0.8 = 0.961.2×0.8=0.96, a 4% loss overall. Three 10% rises: 1.13=1.3311.1^3 = 1.3311.13=1.331, a 33.1% rise, not 30%.

When it does not apply. Adding is a reasonable estimate only when the changes are small, because then ababab is tiny.

49. Undo a percentage change by dividing

The trick. To find the value before a change, divide by the multiplier.

Why it works. If new=old×m\text{new} = \text{old} \times mnew=old×m, then old=new÷m\text{old} = \text{new} \div mold=new÷m.

Example. A price is £91 after a 30% rise. Original: 91÷1.3=7091 \div 1.3 = 7091÷1.3=70.

When it does not apply. Subtracting 30% of the new price is wrong: 91×0.7=63.791 \times 0.7 = 63.791×0.7=63.7. Teachers list this reversal as a frequent misconception (Mr Barton Maths).

50. Keep percentage points and percent change apart

The trick. When a rate moves from 4% to 5%, it rose by 1 percentage point, which is a 25% relative increase.

Why it works. Percentage points are a difference, 5−4=15 - 4 = 15−4=1. Percent change is a ratio, 5−44=0.25\dfrac{5 - 4}{4} = 0.2545−4​=0.25.

Example. An interest rate going from 2% to 3% is a 1-point rise and a 50% relative rise.

When it does not apply. This is a reading trick, not a shortcut. It matters whenever the quantity being changed is itself a percentage.

51. Estimate doubling time with the rule of 72

The trick. At a growth rate of r%r\%r% per period, the doubling time is roughly 72÷r72 \div r72÷r periods.

Why it works. Doubling requires (1+i)t=2(1 + i)^t = 2(1+i)t=2, so t=ln⁡2ln⁡(1+i)t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + i)}t=ln(1+i)ln2​. For small iii, ln⁡(1+i)≈i\ln(1 + i) \approx iln(1+i)≈i, giving t≈0.693i=69.3rt \approx \dfrac{0.693}{i} = \dfrac{69.3}{r}t≈i0.693​=r69.3​. Using 72 instead of 69.3 partly corrects for ln⁡(1+i)\ln(1 + i)ln(1+i) being slightly smaller than iii at typical rates, and 72 has many divisors.

Example. At 6% per year: 72÷6=1272 \div 6 = 1272÷6=12 years. The exact value is ln⁡2/ln⁡1.06≈11.9\ln 2 / \ln 1.06 \approx 11.9ln2/ln1.06≈11.9 years.

52. Memorize a few benchmark fractions

The trick. Know the decimal forms of common fractions: 18=0.125\tfrac{1}{8} = 0.12581​=0.125, 38=0.375\tfrac{3}{8} = 0.37583​=0.375, 58=0.625\tfrac{5}{8} = 0.62585​=0.625, 78=0.875\tfrac{7}{8} = 0.87587​=0.875, 16=0.16‾\tfrac{1}{6} = 0.1\overline{6}61​=0.16, 112=0.083‾\tfrac{1}{12} = 0.08\overline{3}121​=0.083, 116=0.0625\tfrac{1}{16} = 0.0625161​=0.0625.

53. Read sevenths from the cycle 142857

The trick. Every fraction k7\tfrac{k}{7}7k​ (for k=1k = 1k=1 to 666) repeats the digits 142857142857142857 in the same cyclic order. Start where the leading digit matches.

Why it works. In the long division of 1 by 7, the remainders cycle through all of 1,2,…,61, 2, \dots, 61,2,…,6. Starting from a different numerator just starts the same cycle at a different point.

54. Divide by 5 or 25 by multiplying

The trick. n÷5=2n÷10n \div 5 = 2n \div 10n÷5=2n÷10, and n÷25=4n÷100n \div 25 = 4n \div 100n÷25=4n÷100.

Why it works. 15=210\tfrac{1}{5} = \tfrac{2}{10}51​=102​ and 125=4100\tfrac{1}{25} = \tfrac{4}{100}251​=1004​.

55. Compare fractions by cross-multiplying

The trick. To compare ab\tfrac{a}{b}ba​ and cd\tfrac{c}{d}dc​ with positive denominators, compare adadad with bcbcbc.

Why it works. Multiplying both fractions by the positive number bdbdbd preserves the order: ab<cd  ⟺  ad<bc\tfrac{a}{b} < \tfrac{c}{d} \iff ad < bcba​<dc​⟺ad<bc.

56. Add two unit fractions in one line

The trick. 1a+1b=a+bab\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{a + b}{ab}a1​+b1​=aba+b​.

Why it works. Use the common denominator ababab: bab+aab\dfrac{b}{ab} + \dfrac{a}{ab}abb​+aba​.

The trick. Rewrite each term as a difference so that neighbouring terms cancel.

Why it works. 1n(n+1)=1n−1n+1\dfrac{1}{n(n + 1)} = \dfrac{1}{n} - \dfrac{1}{n + 1}n(n+1)1​=n1​−n+11​, so in a sum everything cancels except the first and last pieces.

58. Cancel before you multiply

The trick. Divide out common factors between any numerator and any denominator before multiplying.

Why it works. ab⋅cd=acbd\dfrac{a}{b} \cdot \dfrac{c}{d} = \dfrac{ac}{bd}ba​⋅dc​=bdac​, and a common factor can be removed from acacac and bdbdbd at any stage.

59. Turn a repeating decimal into a fraction

The trick. A block of kkk repeating digits right after the decimal point equals that block over kkk nines.

60. Average by deviations from a guess

The trick. Pick a convenient guess, average the differences from it, and add that to the guess.

Why it works. 1n∑xi=g+1n∑(xi−g)\dfrac{1}{n}\sum x_i = g + \dfrac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - g)n1​∑xi​=g+n1​∑(xi​−g) for any guess ggg.

Estimation and checking

61. Round to one significant figure first

The trick. Round each number to one significant figure and compute an estimate before doing the exact calculation.

Why it works. The relative error of each rounded factor is limited, so the estimate lands in the right order of magnitude.

Example. 412×587≈400×600=240,000412 \times 587 \approx 400 \times 600 = 240{,}000412×587≈400×600=240,000. The exact product is 241,844241{,}844241,844.

When it does not apply. Errors can pile up when every number is rounded in the same direction, and the estimate is not a substitute for the exact answer when precision matters.

62. Use scientific notation for very large or small numbers

The trick. Write numbers as a×10na \times 10^na×10n with 1≤∣a∣<101 \le |a| < 101≤∣a∣<10, multiply the aaa parts and add the exponents (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §1.2).

Why it works. (a×10m)(b×10n)=ab×10m+n(a \times 10^m)(b \times 10^n) = ab \times 10^{m+n}(a×10m)(b×10n)=ab×10m+n by the product rule for exponents.

When it does not apply. Remember to renormalize: 19.2×10919.2 \times 10^919.2×109 is correct but not in standard form.

63. Bracket the answer between bounds

The trick. Round all factors down for a lower bound and all up for an upper bound.

Why it works. For positive numbers, multiplication preserves order: if a1≤a≤a2a_1 \le a \le a_2a1​≤a≤a2​ and b1≤b≤b2b_1 \le b \le b_2b1​≤b≤b2​, then a1b1≤ab≤a2b2a_1 b_1 \le ab \le a_2 b_2a1​b1​≤ab≤a2​b2​.

Example. 410×580=237,800≤412×587≤420×590=247,800410 \times 580 = 237{,}800 \le 412 \times 587 \le 420 \times 590 = 247{,}800410×580=237,800≤412×587≤420×590=247,800.

When it does not apply. With negative numbers or subtraction, the directions change. For a−ba - ba−b, the lower bound uses the smallest aaa and the largest bbb.

64. Count the digits of a product

The trick. The product of an mmm-digit and an nnn-digit whole number has either m+n−1m + n - 1m+n−1 or m+nm + nm+n digits.

Why it works. 10m−1≤a<10m10^{m-1} \le a < 10^m10m−1≤a<10m and 10n−1≤b<10n10^{n-1} \le b < 10^n10n−1≤b<10n, so 10m+n−2≤ab<10m+n10^{m+n-2} \le ab < 10^{m+n}10m+n−2≤ab<10m+n.

Example. 4,321×5674{,}321 \times 5674,321×567 (4 digits times 3 digits) must have 6 or 7 digits. The exact product, 2,450,0072{,}450{,}0072,450,007, has 7.

When it does not apply. It narrows the size to two options; use trick 61 to choose between them.

65. Let the units do the work

The trick. Multiply by conversion factors written as fractions equal to 1, and cancel units like numbers.

Why it works. A factor such as 1000 m1 km\dfrac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}}1 km1000 m​ equals 1, so multiplying by it changes the units but not the quantity.

Example.

90 kmh×1000 m1 km×1 h3600 s=25 ms90\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \frac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} \times \frac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}} = 25\ \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}90 hkm​×1 km1000 m​×3600 s1 h​=25 sm​

When it does not apply. Units confirm the form of an answer, not its numerical correctness. A formula can have the right units and the wrong constant (for example, πr2\pi r^2πr2 versus 2πr22\pi r^22πr2).

66. Test an algebraic step with a number

The trick. After simplifying an expression, substitute a simple value into both the original and the result.

Why it works. If two expressions are identical, they agree for every value of the variable, so one disagreement proves an error.

Example. Is (x+3)2=x2+9(x + 3)^2 = x^2 + 9(x+3)2=x2+9? At x=1x = 1x=1: 16≠1016 \ne 1016=10. The correct expansion is x2+6x+9x^2 + 6x + 9x2+6x+9, which gives 16.

When it does not apply. Agreement at one value does not prove the identity. Avoid test values like 0 and 1, which hide many errors; try two values such as 2 and 3.

67. Check by the inverse operation

The trick. Check a product by dividing, a quotient by multiplying, a sum by subtracting, a root by squaring.

Why it works. Inverse operations undo each other: (a×b)÷b=a(a \times b) \div b = a(a×b)÷b=a when b≠0b \ne 0b=0.

Example. To check 348×27=9396348 \times 27 = 9396348×27=9396, compute 9396÷27=3489396 \div 27 = 3489396÷27=348.

When it does not apply. Squaring checks the magnitude of a root, not its sign: both 333 and −3-3−3 square to 9.

68. Divide using compatible numbers

The trick. Replace the dividend with a nearby number that the divisor divides evenly.

Why it works. Small changes to the dividend change the quotient by the change divided by the divisor.

Example. 4,970÷7≈4,900÷7=7004{,}970 \div 7 \approx 4{,}900 \div 7 = 7004,970÷7≈4,900÷7=700. The exact answer is 710710710, since 70÷7=1070 \div 7 = 1070÷7=10 was dropped.

When it does not apply. It is an estimate. For the exact quotient, add back the adjustment as shown.

69. Add from left to right

The trick. Add the thousands, then the hundreds, tens and units, keeping a running total.

Why it works. Addition is associative and commutative, so place values can be added in any order.

Example. 3,476+2,8583{,}476 + 2{,}8583,476+2,858: 5000+1200+120+14=63345000 + 1200 + 120 + 14 = 63345000+1200+120+14=6334.

70. Subtract from a power of 10 with nines

The trick. To compute 1000−n1000 - n1000−n for a three-digit nnn, subtract each digit from 9 except the last nonzero one, which you subtract from 10.

Why it works. 1000−n=(999−n)+11000 - n = (999 - n) + 11000−n=(999−n)+1, and subtracting from 999 never needs borrowing.

Example. 1000−3671000 - 3671000−367: 9−3=69 - 3 = 69−3=6, 9−6=39 - 6 = 39−6=3, 10−7=310 - 7 = 310−7=3. Answer: 633633633.

Algebra shortcuts

71. Add the first n whole numbers by pairing

The trick. 1+2+⋯+n=n(n+1)21 + 2 + \dots + n = \dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}1+2+⋯+n=2n(n+1)​.

The trick. a+ar+ar2+⋯+arn−1=a rn−1r−1a + ar + ar^2 + \dots + ar^{n-1} = a\,\dfrac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}a+ar+ar2+⋯+arn−1=ar−1rn−1​ (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §13.4).

74. Factor out the common factor first

The trick. When the same factor appears in every term, pull it out before computing.

75. Spot the difference of squares

The trick. Any expression of the form a2−b2a^2 - b^2a2−b2 factors as (a+b)(a−b)(a + b)(a - b)(a+b)(a−b) (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §1.5).
