76. Factor quadratics with the ac method

The trick. Find two numbers whose product is acacac and whose sum is bbb. Split the middle term with them and factor by grouping (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §1.5).

Why it works. If (px+q)(rx+s)(px + q)(rx + s)(px+q)(rx+s) is the factorization, then a=pra = pra=pr, c=qsc = qsc=qs, and b=ps+qrb = ps + qrb=ps+qr. The two middle-term pieces pspsps and qrqrqr multiply to pqrs=acpqrs = acpqrs=ac.

Example. 6x2+11x+46x^2 + 11x + 46x2+11x+4: ac=24ac = 24ac=24, and 3×8=243 \times 8 = 243×8=24 with 3+8=113 + 8 = 113+8=11. So 6x2+3x+8x+4=3x(2x+1)+4(2x+1)=(3x+4)(2x+1)6x^2 + 3x + 8x + 4 = 3x(2x + 1) + 4(2x + 1) = (3x + 4)(2x + 1)6x2+3x+8x+4=3x(2x+1)+4(2x+1)=(3x+4)(2x+1).

When it does not apply. If no integer pair exists, the quadratic does not factor over the integers. Use the quadratic formula instead.

77. Check roots with their sum and product

The trick. For ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0, the roots add to −ba-\dfrac{b}{a}−ab​ and multiply to ca\dfrac{c}{a}ac​.

Why it works. If the roots are rrr and sss, then ax2+bx+c=a(x−r)(x−s)=ax2−a(r+s)x+arsax^2 + bx + c = a(x - r)(x - s) = a x^2 - a(r + s)x + arsax2+bx+c=a(x−r)(x−s)=ax2−a(r+s)x+ars. Compare coefficients.

Example. x2−5x+6=0x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0x2−5x+6=0: the roots sum to 5 and multiply to 6, so they are 2 and 3.

When it does not apply. It identifies roots quickly only when they are small integers. Otherwise use it as a check after solving.

78. Use the discriminant before solving

The trick. Compute b2−4acb^2 - 4acb2−4ac first. Positive: two real roots. Zero: one repeated root. Negative: no real roots (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §2.5).

Why it works. The quadratic formula is x=−b±b2−4ac2ax = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}x=2a−b±b2−4ac​​, and the square root is real only when b2−4ac≥0b^2 - 4ac \ge 0b2−4ac≥0.

Example. 2x2+3x+5=02x^2 + 3x + 5 = 02x2+3x+5=0: 9−40=−31<09 - 40 = -31 < 09−40=−31<0, so there are no real solutions. No need to try factoring.

When it does not apply. Only for quadratics. A perfect-square discriminant also tells you the roots are rational, so factoring will work.

79. Complete the square to find the vertex

The trick. Rewrite x2+bx+cx^2 + bx + cx2+bx+c as (x+b2)2+c−b24\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2 + c - \tfrac{b^2}{4}(x+2b​)2+c−4b2​.

Why it works. Expanding (x+b2)2\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2}\right)^2(x+2b​)2 gives x2+bx+b24x^2 + bx + \tfrac{b^2}{4}x2+bx+4b2​, so subtracting b24\tfrac{b^2}{4}4b2​ restores the original expression (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §2.5).

Example. x2+6x+5=(x+3)2−4x^2 + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)^2 - 4x2+6x+5=(x+3)2−4. The minimum value is −4-4−4 at x=−3x = -3x=−3, and the roots are x=−3±2x = -3 \pm 2x=−3±2, that is, −1-1−1 and −5-5−5.

When it does not apply. If the x2x^2x2 coefficient is not 1, factor it out of the first two terms first.

80. Clear fractions with the least common denominator

The trick. Multiply every term of an equation by the least common denominator before solving.

Why it works. Multiplying both sides of an equation by the same nonzero number keeps it balanced.

Example. x3+x4=7\dfrac{x}{3} + \dfrac{x}{4} = 73x​+4x​=7. Multiply by 12: 4x+3x=844x + 3x = 844x+3x=84, so x=12x = 12x=12.

When it does not apply. Multiply every term, including the right side. With variables in a denominator, check that your solution does not make any denominator zero.

81. Rewrite powers with a common base

The trick. Express all bases as powers of the same prime, then use the exponent rules.

Why it works. aman=am+na^m a^n = a^{m+n}aman=am+n and (am)n=amn(a^m)^n = a^{mn}(am)n=amn (OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e, §1.2).

Example. 45×82=210×26=216=655364^5 \times 8^2 = 2^{10} \times 2^6 = 2^{16} = 6553645×82=210×26=216=65536, and 27293=3636=1\dfrac{27^2}{9^3} = \dfrac{3^6}{3^6} = 193272​=3636​=1.

When it does not apply. Exponent rules work across multiplication, not addition: 23+23=242^3 + 2^3 = 2^423+23=24, not 262^626.

Geometry shortcuts

82. Exterior angle of a triangle

The trick. An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.

Why it works. The interior angles add to 180∘180^\circ180∘ (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §9.3), and the exterior angle is 180∘180^\circ180∘ minus the third interior angle. Both equal A+BA + BA+B.

Example. If two interior angles are 50∘50^\circ50∘ and 60∘60^\circ60∘, the exterior angle at the third vertex is 110∘110^\circ110∘.

When it does not apply. It uses the two remote interior angles, not the adjacent one.

83. Angle sum of any polygon

The trick. The interior angles of an nnn-sided polygon add to (n−2)×180∘(n - 2) \times 180^\circ(n−2)×180∘.

Why it works. Diagonals from one vertex divide a convex polygon into n−2n - 2n−2 triangles, each contributing 180∘180^\circ180∘.

Example. A hexagon's angles add to 720∘720^\circ720∘, so each angle of a regular hexagon is 120∘120^\circ120∘.

When it does not apply. The "divide by nnn" step only applies to regular polygons. The sum itself also holds for non-convex simple polygons.

84. Recognize Pythagorean triples and their multiples

The trick. Learn 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and 7-24-25. Any multiple of a triple is also a triple.

Why it works. If a2+b2=c2a^2 + b^2 = c^2a2+b2=c2, then (ka)2+(kb)2=k2c2=(kc)2(ka)^2 + (kb)^2 = k^2 c^2 = (kc)^2(ka)2+(kb)2=k2c2=(kc)2.

Example. A right triangle with legs 15 and 20 is 3-4-5 scaled by 5, so the hypotenuse is 25.

When it does not apply. Only for right triangles, and only when the sides match a known triple. Otherwise compute a2+b2\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}a2+b2​.

85. Generate Pythagorean triples

The trick. For whole numbers m>n>0m > n > 0m>n>0, the numbers m2−n2m^2 - n^2m2−n2, 2mn2mn2mn and m2+n2m^2 + n^2m2+n2 form a Pythagorean triple.

Why it works.

(m2−n2)2+(2mn)2=m4+2m2n2+n4=(m2+n2)2(m^2 - n^2)^2 + (2mn)^2 = m^4 + 2m^2n^2 + n^4 = (m^2 + n^2)^2(m2−n2)2+(2mn)2=m4+2m2n2+n4=(m2+n2)2

Example. m=3,n=2m = 3, n = 2m=3,n=2 gives 5, 12, 13. m=4,n=1m = 4, n = 1m=4,n=1 gives 15, 8, 17.

When it does not apply. Some choices give scaled copies (for example m=3,n=1m = 3, n = 1m=3,n=1 gives 8, 6, 10). To get every primitive triple, mmm and nnn must be coprime and not both odd.

86. Use the special right triangles

The trick. In a 45∘45^\circ45∘-45∘45^\circ45∘-90∘90^\circ90∘ triangle, the sides are in the ratio 1:1:21 : 1 : \sqrt{2}1:1:2​. In a 30∘30^\circ30∘-60∘60^\circ60∘-90∘90^\circ90∘ triangle, they are 1:3:21 : \sqrt{3} : 21:3​:2.

Why it works. The first is half a square, so the Pythagorean theorem gives a diagonal of 12+12=2\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2}12+12​=2​. The second is half an equilateral triangle of side 2, with height 22−12=3\sqrt{2^2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{3}22−12​=3​.

Example. A 45∘45^\circ45∘ right triangle with leg 7 has hypotenuse 727\sqrt{2}72​. A 30∘30^\circ30∘-60∘60^\circ60∘-90∘90^\circ90∘ triangle with hypotenuse 10 has legs 555 and 535\sqrt{3}53​.

When it does not apply. Only for those exact angles. Match the shortest side to the smallest angle.

87. Distance between two points is Pythagoras

The trick. The distance between (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​) and (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2)(x2​,y2​) is (x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2\sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}(x2​−x1​)2+(y2​−y1​)2​. Look for a familiar triple in the differences.

Why it works. The horizontal and vertical differences are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the segment (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §9.3).

Example. From (1,2)(1, 2)(1,2) to (7,10)(7, 10)(7,10): differences 666 and 888, a 3-4-5 triple doubled, so the distance is 101010.

When it does not apply. It is the straight-line distance in a flat plane, not a distance along streets or on a sphere.

88. Scale factors square for area and cube for volume

The trick. If every length is multiplied by kkk, areas are multiplied by k2k^2k2 and volumes by k3k^3k3.

Why it works. Similar figures have proportional sides (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §9.3). Area is a product of two lengths and volume a product of three.

Example. A 12-inch pizza versus an 8-inch pizza: k=1.5k = 1.5k=1.5, so the area ratio is 1.52=2.251.5^2 = 2.251.52=2.25. Doubling every edge of a box multiplies its volume by 8.

When it does not apply. The shapes must be similar (every length scaled by the same factor). Stretching only one dimension does not follow this rule.

89. Trapezoid area: average base times height

The trick. Area = average of the two parallel sides × height.

Why it works. A=12h(b+B)A = \tfrac{1}{2}h(b + B)A=21​h(b+B) (OpenStax Prealgebra 2e, §9.4), which is b+B2×h\dfrac{b + B}{2} \times h2b+B​×h. Two copies of the trapezoid, one rotated, form a parallelogram with base b+Bb + Bb+B.

Example. Bases 6 and 10, height 4: 8×4=328 \times 4 = 328×4=32.

When it does not apply. The height is the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides, not a slanted side length.

90. Shoelace formula for a polygon's area from its corners

The trick. For vertices (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​) listed in order around the shape,

A=12∣∑i=1n(xiyi+1−xi+1yi)∣A = \frac{1}{2}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i\right)\right|A=21​​i=1∑n​(xi​yi+1​−xi+1​yi​)​

where (xn+1,yn+1)=(x1,y1)(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) = (x_1, y_1)(xn+1​,yn+1​)=(x1​,y1​).

Why it works. Each term is twice the signed area of the triangle formed by the origin and one edge. Adding them around the boundary cancels everything outside the polygon.

Example. Triangle (0,0),(4,0),(1,3)(0, 0), (4, 0), (1, 3)(0,0),(4,0),(1,3): (0−0)+(12−0)+(0−0)=12(0 - 0) + (12 - 0) + (0 - 0) = 12(0−0)+(12−0)+(0−0)=12, so A=6A = 6A=6. Check: base 4, height 3, 12×4×3=6\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 3 = 621​×4×3=6.

When it does not apply. The vertices must be in order around the boundary, and the polygon must not cross itself.

91. Count the diagonals of a polygon

The trick. An nnn-sided polygon has n(n−3)2\dfrac{n(n - 3)}{2}2n(n−3)​ diagonals.

Why it works. Each vertex connects to n−3n - 3n−3 others by a diagonal (not itself or its two neighbours). That counts each diagonal twice, once from each end.

Example. An octagon has 8×52=20\dfrac{8 \times 5}{2} = 2028×5​=20 diagonals.

When it does not apply. It counts diagonals, not their intersections or the regions they create.

Problem-solving strategies

These are heuristics in the sense Pólya used the word: suggestions that often help, not guarantees (Princeton University Press). Each one still gets a reason and a worked example.

92. Name the unknown before computing

The trick. Pólya's first phase is understanding the problem: state what is unknown, what is given, and what condition links them (Wikipedia summary of How to Solve It). Then write that condition as an equation.

Why it works. Many fast wrong answers come from computing with the given numbers before deciding what the answer represents.

Example. A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together, and the bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. Let the ball cost bbb. Then b+(b+1.00)=1.10b + (b + 1.00) = 1.10b+(b+1.00)=1.10, so 2b=0.102b = 0.102b=0.10 and b=0.05b = 0.05b=0.05. The ball costs 5 cents, not 10.

When it does not apply. This is a habit, not a formula. It costs a few seconds on simple problems and saves the most on worded ones.

93. Draw a figure

The trick. Sketch the situation, label the known lengths and angles, and mark the unknown. "Draw a figure" is one of the heuristics in Pólya's dictionary (Wikipedia summary).

Why it works. A diagram can reveal a known structure, such as a right triangle, that the words hide.

Example. A 10 m ladder leans against a wall with its foot 6 m out. The sketch is a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and leg 6, which is 3-4-5 doubled, so the ladder reaches 8 m up the wall.

When it does not apply. A sketch is not a proof. A carelessly drawn figure can suggest equal lengths or right angles that are not actually given.

94. Work backwards from the result

The trick. When the final state is known, reverse each step in the opposite order using inverse operations. Working backwards is one of Pólya's named heuristics (Princeton University Press).

Why it works. Each operation has an inverse, and undoing the steps in reverse order recovers the starting value.

Example. "I double a number, add 7 and get 31." Undo: 31−7=2431 - 7 = 2431−7=24, then 24÷2=1224 \div 2 = 1224÷2=12. Check: 2×12+7=312 \times 12 + 7 = 312×12+7=31.

When it does not apply. Steps without a unique inverse block the method. If the step was "square it", working backwards gives two candidates.

95. Specialize: try small cases first

The trick. Solve the problem for small values, then look for the rule. Pólya lists specialization as a heuristic (Wikipedia summary).

Why it works. Small cases are easy to count directly and often reveal a structure you can then prove.

Example. How many handshakes when 10 people each shake hands once with everyone else? With 2, 3, 4 people: 1, 3, 6. Each of nnn people shakes n−1n - 1n−1 hands, and each handshake is counted twice, giving n(n−1)2\dfrac{n(n - 1)}{2}2n(n−1)​. For 10 people: 454545.

When it does not apply. A pattern from small cases must still be justified. Patterns can break later; the reasoning step is what makes the answer reliable.

96. Look for a repeating pattern

The trick. When a calculation repeats, find the cycle length and use the remainder.

Why it works. Last digits of powers depend only on the previous last digit, so they must eventually repeat.

Example. The last digit of 720267^{2026}72026: the last digits of 71,72,73,747^1, 7^2, 7^3, 7^471,72,73,74 are 7, 9, 3, 1, then repeat. Since 2026=4×506+22026 = 4 \times 506 + 22026=4×506+2, the last digit matches 727^272, which is 9.

When it does not apply. You must confirm the cycle actually repeats, and line up the remainder correctly (a remainder of 0 corresponds to the 4th position, not the first).

97. Use symmetry

The trick. When a problem treats two quantities the same way, try the case where they are equal, then measure how far you are from it.

Why it works. For two numbers with a fixed sum 2m2m2m, write them as m+dm + dm+d and m−dm - dm−d. Their product is m2−d2m^2 - d^2m2−d2, which is largest when d=0d = 0d=0.

Example. Two numbers add to 20. Their product is at most 10×10=10010 \times 10 = 10010×10=100; for example 12×8=100−4=9612 \times 8 = 100 - 4 = 9612×8=100−4=96.

When it does not apply. Symmetry suggests where to look, not that the symmetric case is the answer. Check whether the problem's conditions are truly symmetric.

98. Assume one extreme, then adjust

The trick. For "two kinds of things" problems, assume everything is of one kind, then swap items one at a time to fix the total. This is systematic guess-and-check.

Why it works. Each swap changes the total by the same fixed amount, so the number of swaps is the shortfall divided by that amount. It is the same as solving a system of two linear equations.

Example. A farm has 20 animals (chickens and cows) with 56 legs. If all 20 were chickens there would be 40 legs. Each cow adds 2 legs, so there are (56−40)÷2=8(56 - 40) \div 2 = 8(56−40)÷2=8 cows and 12 chickens. Check: 12×2+8×4=5612 \times 2 + 8 \times 4 = 5612×2+8×4=56.

When it does not apply. It works when each item contributes a fixed amount. With three or more kinds, you need more information.

99. Introduce an auxiliary variable

The trick. Replace a repeated expression with a new letter to turn an unfamiliar problem into a familiar one. Pólya calls this an auxiliary element or auxiliary problem (Wikipedia summary).

Why it works. The substitution does not change the solutions; it only changes how they look.

Example. x4−5x2+4=0x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0x4−5x2+4=0. Let u=x2u = x^2u=x2: u2−5u+4=0u^2 - 5u + 4 = 0u2−5u+4=0, so u=1u = 1u=1 or u=4u = 4u=4. Then x=±1x = \pm 1x=±1 or x=±2x = \pm 2x=±2.

When it does not apply. Translate back at the end, and discard values that are impossible for the substitution. Here u=x2u = x^2u=x2 cannot be negative for real xxx.

100. Decompose and recombine

The trick. Break a hard shape or problem into easy pieces, solve each, and recombine. "Decomposing and recombining" is another of Pólya's heuristics (Wikipedia summary).

Why it works. Area is additive for non-overlapping pieces; more generally, a sum of independent parts can be found part by part.

Example. An L-shaped floor that is a 10×610 \times 610×6 rectangle with a 4×34 \times 34×3 corner removed has area 60−12=4860 - 12 = 4860−12=48. Splitting it into a 10×310 \times 310×3 and a 6×36 \times 36×3 rectangle gives the same 30+18=4830 + 18 = 4830+18=48.

When it does not apply. The pieces must not overlap or leave gaps. If they overlap, subtract the overlap once.

101. Look back

The trick. After finishing, check the answer, check the argument, and ask whether the method could solve related problems. This is the fourth phase of Pólya's method (Princeton University Press).

Why it works. Checks such as substitution, estimation (trick 61) or casting out nines (trick 42) catch errors cheaply. Asking "where else does this work?" is how individual tricks become a toolkit.

Example. For the equation in trick 80, substitute x=12x = 12x=12: 123+124=4+3=7\tfrac{12}{3} + \tfrac{12}{4} = 4 + 3 = 7312​+412​=4+3=7. Correct. Looking back also shows that the "clear the denominators" step is the same idea used to compare fractions in trick 55.

When it does not apply. It always applies, but it takes time; under a strict time limit, prioritize a quick estimate or substitution check over a full review.

Common mistakes

Most errors with shortcuts come from using a trick outside the conditions that make its algebra true. The most frequent ones:

  • Splitting a square over a sum. (a+b)2≠a2+b2(a + b)^2 \ne a^2 + b^2(a+b)2=a2+b2; the middle term 2ab2ab2ab is required (trick 66). Likewise, a+b≠a+b\sqrt{a + b} \ne \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}a+b​=a​+b​ (trick 27).
  • Adding percentages that should multiply. Successive changes multiply (trick 48), and a reverse percentage needs division, not subtraction (trick 49). These two errors appear in teachers' lists of common misconceptions (Mr Barton Maths).
  • Combining divisibility tests that share a factor. Passing the tests for 4 and 6 does not prove divisibility by 24 (trick 36).
  • Trusting a passed check as proof. Casting out nines misses swapped digits and extra zeros (Wolfram MathWorld). Pair it with an estimate.
  • Ignoring the carry. Tricks 4, 10, 11 and 16 all produce two-digit pieces that can overflow into the next place.
  • Stretching a trick beyond its range. Squaring near 50 or 100 is clean only within 9 of the base (tricks 18 and 19); the rule of 72 is only an approximation (trick 51).
  • Using one check value of 0 or 1. These values hide many algebra errors (trick 66).

Next steps

If you want to go from shortcuts to fluency, these articles build on the same foundations:

  • Math formulas every student should know: a reference for the identities used throughout this list.
  • Algebra problems with solutions for beginners: practice tricks 71 to 81 on full worked problems.
  • Probability and statistics with real-world examples: estimation and percentage reasoning applied to data.
  • Linear algebra concepts for machine learning: where scaling, distance and decomposition ideas lead next.
  • All Mathematics articles on this site.

A practical approach: pick three or four tricks that match the arithmetic you do most often, practise them until they are automatic, and always finish with a quick check (tricks 42, 61 and 101).

References

  1. Marecek, L., Anthony-Smith, M., and Honeycutt Mathis, A. Prealgebra 2e. OpenStax, 2020. Sections 2.4 Find Multiples and Factors, 6.1 Understand Percent, 9.3 Use Properties of Angles, Triangles, and the Pythagorean Theorem, 9.4 Use Properties of Rectangles, Triangles, and Trapezoids.
  2. Abramson, J. Algebra and Trigonometry 2e. OpenStax, 2021. Sections 1.2 Exponents and Scientific Notation, 1.4 Polynomials, 1.5 Factoring Polynomials, 2.5 Quadratic Equations, 13.4 Series and Their Notations.
  3. Pólya, G. How to Solve It. Princeton University Press, 1945; Princeton Science Library edition 2014. Publisher's page.
  4. "How to Solve It." Wikipedia. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Solve_It. Used as a secondary summary of the book's four phases and heuristics.
  5. Weisstein, E. W. "Divisibility Tests." MathWorld, Wolfram Research. mathworld.wolfram.com/DivisibilityTests.html.
  6. Weisstein, E. W. "Casting Out Nines." MathWorld, Wolfram Research. mathworld.wolfram.com/CastingOutNines.html.
  7. Bogomolny, A. "Divisibility by 7, 11, and 13." Cut the Knot. cut-the-knot.org/blue/div7-11-13.shtml.
  8. Cook, J. D. "Test for divisibility by 13." 10 November 2020. johndcook.com.
  9. "Probing Questions: Percentage Increase and Decrease." Mr Barton Maths. mrbartonmaths.com. Teacher resource on common misconceptions.
  10. "Does the human calculator stuff really work?" Physics Forums, thread started 5 December 2016. physicsforums.com. Community discussion, cited only for practitioners' opinions.

title: 100 Best Probability and Statistics Examples for Real-World Applications
description: 100 worked probability and statistics examples, from medical tests and A/B tests to polls and quality control, each solved step by step.
author: BlogAI Editors
html:
Probability and statistics are easiest to learn when every formula is attached to a decision someone actually has to make: should a patient worry about a positive test, did a website change really lift sales, how many people does a survey need? This article collects 100 short, fully worked examples arranged from basic probability to the paradoxes that catch out experienced analysts.

Each example follows the same pattern: the scenario, the concept it uses, the computation step by step, and a one-line interpretation. Unless a figure is explicitly cited, the numbers are illustrative: they were chosen to make the arithmetic clear, not taken from real studies. The only real data set used here is the 1973 Berkeley admissions data in example 96. Every result was recomputed with Python (NumPy and SciPy) before publication.

Formulas and conventions follow standard references, mainly OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e and the NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods.

Basic probability

These examples use the classical definition of probability (favorable outcomes divided by equally likely outcomes), the complement rule, and counting.

1. Rolling a six in a board game

Scenario: A board game lets you leave the starting square only on a six. Concept: Equally likely outcomes.

P(6)=favorable outcomespossible outcomes=16≈0.167P(6) = \frac{\text{favorable outcomes}}{\text{possible outcomes}} = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167P(6)=possible outcomesfavorable outcomes​=61​≈0.167

Interpretation: On average, one turn in six lets you start moving.

2. Rolling a total of seven with two dice

Scenario: Many dice games pay out on a total of seven. Concept: Counting outcomes in a sample space of 6×6=366 \times 6 = 366×6=36 ordered pairs.

The pairs that sum to 7 are (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1):

P(sum=7)=636=16≈0.167P(\text{sum} = 7) = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167P(sum=7)=366​=61​≈0.167

Interpretation: Seven is the most likely total because more pairs produce it than any other sum.

3. Drawing a heart or a king

Scenario: A magician asks you to draw a card that is either a heart or a king. Concept: Addition rule for overlapping events.

P(H∪K)=P(H)+P(K)−P(H∩K)=1352+452−152=1652≈0.308P(H \cup K) = P(H) + P(K) - P(H \cap K) = \frac{13}{52} + \frac{4}{52} - \frac{1}{52} = \frac{16}{52} \approx 0.308P(H∪K)=P(H)+P(K)−P(H∩K)=5213​+524​−521​=5216​≈0.308

Interpretation: Subtract the king of hearts once, or it is counted twice.

4. At least one six in four rolls

Scenario: A classic gambling bet: will at least one six appear in four rolls of a die? Concept: Complement rule, P(at least one)=1−P(none)P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})P(at least one)=1−P(none).

1−(56)4=1−0.4823=0.51771 - \left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^4 = 1 - 0.4823 = 0.51771−(65​)4=1−0.4823=0.5177

By contrast, getting at least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice has probability 1−(35/36)24≈0.49141 - (35/36)^{24} \approx 0.49141−(35/36)24≈0.4914.

Interpretation: The first bet is slightly favorable and the second slightly unfavorable, even though both "feel" similar.

5. Guessing a four-digit PIN

Scenario: A phone locks after three wrong PIN attempts. Suppose the PIN was chosen uniformly at random. Concept: Equally likely outcomes without repetition of guesses.

P(success in 3 guesses)=310 000=0.0003P(\text{success in 3 guesses}) = \frac{3}{10\,000} = 0.0003P(success in 3 guesses)=100003​=0.0003

Interpretation: Lockouts keep random guessing nearly hopeless; real PINs are not uniform, which is why common PINs are riskier.

6. The birthday problem in a meeting room

Scenario: What is the chance that at least two of 23 colleagues share a birthday? Assume 365 equally likely birthdays and ignore leap years. Concept: Complement rule with a product of probabilities.

P(no match)=365365⋅364365⋯343365≈0.4927P(\text{no match}) = \frac{365}{365} \cdot \frac{364}{365} \cdots \frac{343}{365} \approx 0.4927P(no match)=365365​⋅365364​⋯365343​≈0.4927 P(at least one match)=1−0.4927≈0.5073P(\text{at least one match}) = 1 - 0.4927 \approx 0.5073P(at least one match)=1−0.4927≈0.5073

With 50 people the probability rises to about 0.9704.

Interpretation: Coincidences are far more common than intuition suggests because the number of pairs grows quickly.

7. Winning a 6-of-49 lottery

Scenario: A lottery draws 6 numbers from 49, and order does not matter. Concept: Combinations.

(496)=49!6! 43!=13 983 816\binom{49}{6} = \frac{49!}{6!\,43!} = 13\,983\,816(649​)=6!43!49!​=13983816

Interpretation: One ticket has a 1 in 13,983,816 chance of matching all six numbers.

8. Redundant servers

Scenario: A website runs on two servers. Suppose each is down 1% of the time, independently. The site fails only if both are down. Concept: Multiplication rule for independent events.

P(both down)=0.01×0.01=0.0001,P(site up)=0.9999P(\text{both down}) = 0.01 \times 0.01 = 0.0001, \qquad P(\text{site up}) = 0.9999P(both down)=0.01×0.01=0.0001,P(site up)=0.9999

Interpretation: Redundancy works only if failures are truly independent; a shared power supply would break this calculation.

9. Components in series

Scenario: A device needs three parts to work, each with an assumed reliability of 0.98, failing independently. Concept: Series reliability is a product.

R=0.983=0.941192R = 0.98^3 = 0.941192R=0.983=0.941192

Interpretation: Chaining parts erodes reliability: three good parts give a system that fails almost 6% of the time.

10. Counting license plates

Scenario: A plate format uses three letters followed by three digits. Concept: Fundamental counting principle.

263×103=17 576×1000=17 576 00026^3 \times 10^3 = 17\,576 \times 1000 = 17\,576\,000263×103=17576×1000=17576000

Interpretation: The format supports about 17.6 million distinct plates.

11. Podium finishes in a race

Scenario: Eight runners compete; how many different gold–silver–bronze outcomes are possible? Concept: Permutations (order matters).

P(8,3)=8×7×6=336P(8, 3) = 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336P(8,3)=8×7×6=336

Interpretation: A prediction of the exact podium has a 1 in 336 chance if all orders were equally likely.

12. Coffee and tea drinkers in a survey

Scenario: Suppose 60% of employees drink coffee, 30% drink tea, and 20% drink both. Concept: Addition rule.

P(C∪T)=0.60+0.30−0.20=0.70,P(neither)=0.30P(C \cup T) = 0.60 + 0.30 - 0.20 = 0.70, \qquad P(\text{neither}) = 0.30P(C∪T)=0.60+0.30−0.20=0.70,P(neither)=0.30

Interpretation: A break room stocking both drinks covers 70% of staff.

Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem

Conditional probability P(A∣B)P(A \mid B)P(A∣B) is the probability of AAA once you know BBB happened. Bayes' theorem reverses the condition:

P(A∣B)=P(B∣A) P(A)P(B)P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(B∣A)P(A)​

13. A positive medical screening test

Scenario: Suppose a condition affects 1% of people, a test is 95% sensitive (detects 95% of true cases) and 90% specific (correctly clears 90% of healthy people). A person tests positive. Concept: Bayes' theorem and base rates.

Think of 10,000 people: 100 have the condition and 95 of them test positive; 9,900 do not, and 10% of them, 990, also test positive.

P(condition∣+)=9595+990=951085≈0.0876P(\text{condition} \mid +) = \frac{95}{95 + 990} = \frac{95}{1085} \approx 0.0876P(condition∣+)=95+99095​=108595​≈0.0876

Interpretation: With a rare condition, most positives are false positives; a positive result means "investigate further," not "diagnosed."

14. A second positive test

Scenario: The same person takes the test again and is positive again. Assume the two results are independent given the true status (real repeat tests often are not). Concept: Sequential Bayesian updating; yesterday's posterior is today's prior.

P=0.0876×0.950.0876×0.95+0.9124×0.10=0.08320.0832+0.0912≈0.477P = \frac{0.0876 \times 0.95}{0.0876 \times 0.95 + 0.9124 \times 0.10} = \frac{0.0832}{0.0832 + 0.0912} \approx 0.477P=0.0876×0.95+0.9124×0.100.0876×0.95​=0.0832+0.09120.0832​≈0.477

Interpretation: Two positives raise the probability from about 9% to about 48%, which is why confirmatory testing matters.

15. A spam filter and the word "free"

Scenario: Suppose 40% of email is spam, the word "free" appears in 25% of spam and 2% of legitimate mail. Concept: Bayes' theorem for classification.

P(spam∣free)=0.40×0.250.40×0.25+0.60×0.02=0.1000.112≈0.893P(\text{spam} \mid \text{free}) = \frac{0.40 \times 0.25}{0.40 \times 0.25 + 0.60 \times 0.02} = \frac{0.100}{0.112} \approx 0.893P(spam∣free)=0.40×0.25+0.60×0.020.40×0.25​=0.1120.100​≈0.893

Interpretation: One word moves the spam probability from 40% to about 89%; real filters combine many such clues.

16. Workplace drug testing

Scenario: Suppose 5% of applicants use a substance, and the test is 99% sensitive and 98% specific. Concept: Positive predictive value.

P(user∣+)=0.05×0.990.05×0.99+0.95×0.02=0.04950.0685≈0.723P(\text{user} \mid +) = \frac{0.05 \times 0.99}{0.05 \times 0.99 + 0.95 \times 0.02} = \frac{0.0495}{0.0685} \approx 0.723P(user∣+)=0.05×0.99+0.95×0.020.05×0.99​=0.06850.0495​≈0.723

Interpretation: Even an excellent test leaves about 28% of positives as false alarms at this base rate.

17. Product returns from a contingency table

Scenario: An online store sold 1,000 orders: 200 shoe orders (50 returned) and 800 other orders (40 returned). Concept: Conditional probability from counts, and why the order of conditioning matters.

P(return∣shoes)=50200=0.25,P(shoes∣return)=5090≈0.556P(\text{return} \mid \text{shoes}) = \frac{50}{200} = 0.25, \qquad P(\text{shoes} \mid \text{return}) = \frac{50}{90} \approx 0.556P(return∣shoes)=20050​=0.25,P(shoes∣return)=9050​≈0.556

Interpretation: A quarter of shoe orders come back, but more than half of all returns are shoes. These answer different questions.

18. The Monty Hall game show

Scenario: A prize is behind one of three doors. You pick one; the host, who knows where the prize is, always opens a different, empty door and offers a switch. Concept: Conditional probability with an informed host.

Your first pick is right with probability 1/31/31/3. The host never reveals the prize, so switching wins whenever your first pick was wrong:

P(win by switching)=1−13=23P(\text{win by switching}) = 1 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}P(win by switching)=1−31​=32​

Interpretation: Switching doubles your chances, but only because the host's choice is constrained by knowledge.

19. Which factory made the defective part?

Scenario: Factory A makes 60% of parts with a 2% defect rate; factory B makes 40% with a 5% defect rate (illustrative). Concept: Law of total probability, then Bayes.

P(D)=0.60×0.02+0.40×0.05=0.012+0.020=0.032P(D) = 0.60 \times 0.02 + 0.40 \times 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032P(D)=0.60×0.02+0.40×0.05=0.012+0.020=0.032 P(A∣D)=0.0120.032=0.375P(A \mid D) = \frac{0.012}{0.032} = 0.375P(A∣D)=0.0320.012​=0.375

Interpretation: Although A makes most parts, a defective part is more likely (62.5%) to come from B.

20. Rain and a late commute

Scenario: Suppose it rains on 30% of days; you are late 40% of the time when it rains and 10% when it is dry. Concept: Total probability and reverse conditioning.

P(L)=0.3×0.4+0.7×0.1=0.19,P(rain∣L)=0.120.19≈0.632P(L) = 0.3 \times 0.4 + 0.7 \times 0.1 = 0.19, \qquad P(\text{rain} \mid L) = \frac{0.12}{0.19} \approx 0.632P(L)=0.3×0.4+0.7×0.1=0.19,P(rain∣L)=0.190.12​≈0.632

Interpretation: If you were late, it probably rained, even though most days are dry.

21. Is device type independent of buying?

Scenario: Of 1,000 visitors, 400 used mobile (60 bought) and 600 used desktop (90 bought). Concept: Independence means P(A∣B)=P(A)P(A \mid B) = P(A)P(A∣B)=P(A).

P(buy)=1501000=0.15,P(buy∣mobile)=60400=0.15,P(buy∣desktop)=90600=0.15P(\text{buy}) = \frac{150}{1000} = 0.15, \quad P(\text{buy} \mid \text{mobile}) = \frac{60}{400} = 0.15, \quad P(\text{buy} \mid \text{desktop}) = \frac{90}{600} = 0.15P(buy)=1000150​=0.15,P(buy∣mobile)=40060​=0.15,P(buy∣desktop)=60090​=0.15

Interpretation: In this sample, device type tells you nothing about whether someone buys.

22. Credit card fraud alerts

Scenario: Suppose 0.1% of transactions are fraudulent, and a detector flags 99% of fraud and 1% of legitimate transactions. Concept: Base rates in rare-event detection.

P(fraud∣flag)=0.001×0.990.001×0.99+0.999×0.01=0.000990.01098≈0.090P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{flag}) = \frac{0.001 \times 0.99}{0.001 \times 0.99 + 0.999 \times 0.01} = \frac{0.00099}{0.01098} \approx 0.090P(fraud∣flag)=0.001×0.99+0.999×0.010.001×0.99​=0.010980.00099​≈0.090

Interpretation: About nine in ten alerts are false; fraud teams need a cheap second check, not automatic blocking.

23. The prosecutor's fallacy

Scenario: Suppose a forensic trait matches by chance with probability 1 in 1,000,000, and the crime occurred in a city of 5,000,000 people. A suspect matches and there is no other evidence. Concept: Confusing P(match∣innocent)P(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent})P(match∣innocent) with P(innocent∣match)P(\text{innocent} \mid \text{match})P(innocent∣match).

Expected innocent matches: 4 999 999×10−6≈54\,999\,999 \times 10^{-6} \approx 54999999×10−6≈5. With one true culprit also matching:

P(guilty∣match)≈11+5≈0.167P(\text{guilty} \mid \text{match}) \approx \frac{1}{1 + 5} \approx 0.167P(guilty∣match)≈1+51​≈0.167

Interpretation: "One in a million" does not mean "a million to one guilty"; in a large population, chance matches add up.

24. The two-child puzzle

Scenario: A family has two children and at least one is a boy. What is the chance both are boys? Assume each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl, independently. Concept: Conditioning shrinks the sample space.

Equally likely families: BB, BG, GB, GG. Knowing "at least one boy" removes GG:

P(BB∣at least one B)=13P(BB \mid \text{at least one B}) = \frac{1}{3}P(BB∣at least one B)=31​

Interpretation: The exact wording of what you know changes the answer; this is a common source of disagreement.

A binomial experiment has a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same success probability ppp. Its mean is npnpnp and its standard deviation is np(1−p)\sqrt{np(1-p)}np(1−p)​.

25. Free throws in basketball

Scenario: A player makes 70% of free throws (assumed constant and independent). What is the chance of exactly 7 makes in 10 attempts? Concept: Binomial probability.

P(X=7)=(107)(0.7)7(0.3)3=120×0.08235×0.027≈0.267P(X = 7) = \binom{10}{7}(0.7)^7(0.3)^3 = 120 \times 0.08235 \times 0.027 \approx 0.267P(X=7)=(710​)(0.7)7(0.3)3=120×0.08235×0.027≈0.267

26. Finding at least one defect in a sample

Scenario: Suppose 2% of items are defective. An inspector checks 50. Concept: Binomial complement.

28. Email campaign clicks

μ=np=30,σ=1000×0.03×0.97≈5.39\mu = np = 30, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{1000 \times 0.03 \times 0.97} \approx 5.39μ=np=30,σ=1000×0.03×0.97​≈5.39

29. Calls to a help desk

31. Typos in a document

32. Sales calls until the first sale

E[calls]=1p=5,P(first sale on call 3)=0.82×0.2=0.128E[\text{calls}] = \frac{1}{p} = 5, \qquad P(\text{first sale on call 3}) = 0.8^2 \times 0.2 = 0.128E[calls]=p1​=5,P(first sale on call 3)=0.82×0.2=0.128

34. Acceptance sampling from a small lot

35. Matching exactly three lottery numbers

The normal distribution

The normal distribution has the familiar bell shape, with mean μ\muμ and standard deviation σ\sigmaσ (NIST section 1.3.6.6.1). A z-score, z=(x−μ)/σz = (x - \mu)/\sigmaz=(x−μ)/σ, counts how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean, and the empirical rule says about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values fall within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations. Below, Φ\PhiΦ is the standard normal cumulative probability.

Scenario: Suppose adult heights in a group are normal with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 7 cm. Where does 185 cm fall? Concept: z-score and percentile.

z=185−1707≈2.14,Φ(2.14)≈0.984z = \frac{185 - 170}{7} \approx 2.14, \qquad \Phi(2.14) \approx 0.984z=7185−170​≈2.14,Φ(2.14)≈0.984

44. Total time for a two-step task

45. Comparing scores on two different tests

Scenario: Ana scores 650 on a test with mean 500 and SD 100; Ben scores 28 on a test with mean 21 and SD 5. Concept: Standardizing puts different scales on one ruler.

zAna=650−500100=1.5,zBen=28−215=1.4z_{\text{Ana}} = \frac{650 - 500}{100} = 1.5, \qquad z_{\text{Ben}} = \frac{28 - 21}{5} = 1.4zAna​=100650−500​=1.5,zBen​=528−21​=1.4

Interpretation: Ana did slightly better relative to her test-takers.

46. Airline overbooking

Scenario: A flight has 200 seats and sells 210 tickets. Suppose each passenger shows up independently with probability 0.94. Concept: Binomial tail, checked with a normal approximation.

μ=210×0.94=197.4,σ=210×0.94×0.06≈3.44\mu = 210 \times 0.94 = 197.4, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{210 \times 0.94 \times 0.06} \approx 3.44μ=210×0.94=197.4,σ=210×0.94×0.06​≈3.44 P(X≥201)≈P ⁣(Z>200.5−197.43.44)=P(Z>0.90)≈0.184(exact: 0.186)P(X \ge 201) \approx P\!\left(Z > \frac{200.5 - 197.4}{3.44}\right) = P(Z > 0.90) \approx 0.184 \quad (\text{exact: } 0.186)P(X≥201)≈P(Z>3.44200.5−197.4​)=P(Z>0.90)≈0.184(exact: 0.186)

Expectation and variance

The expected value E[X]=∑x P(x)E[X] = \sum x \, P(x)E[X]=∑xP(x) is the long-run average; variance measures spread around it.

47. Is a raffle ticket worth it?

Scenario: A charity sells 1,000 tickets at $5 each for a single $2,000 prize. Concept: Expected value of a gamble.

E[net]=0.001×1995+0.999×(−5)=1.995−4.995=−3E[\text{net}] = 0.001 \times 1995 + 0.999 \times (-5) = 1.995 - 4.995 = -3E[net]=0.001×1995+0.999×(−5)=1.995−4.995=−3

Interpretation: Each ticket loses $3 on average; the buyer is effectively donating.

48. Pricing an insurance policy

Scenario: Suppose a policy pays $20,000 with probability 1% per year. Concept: Expected payout as the break-even premium.

E[payout]=0.01×20 000=200E[\text{payout}] = 0.01 \times 20\,000 = 200E[payout]=0.01×20000=200

Interpretation: A premium of $250 would leave the insurer an expected $50 per policy to cover costs and risk.

49. A bet on red in American roulette

Scenario: An American wheel has 38 pockets, 18 red. A $1 bet on red pays $1. Concept: Expected value and house edge.

E=1838(1)+2038(−1)=−238≈−0.0526E = \frac{18}{38}(1) + \frac{20}{38}(-1) = -\frac{2}{38} \approx -0.0526E=3818​(1)+3820​(−1)=−382​≈−0.0526

Interpretation: The player loses about 5.3 cents per dollar bet in the long run.

50. Extended warranty

Scenario: A two-year warranty costs $150. Suppose the chance of needing a $600 repair in that time is 10%. Concept: Comparing expected cost with price.

E[repair cost]=0.10×600=60<150E[\text{repair cost}] = 0.10 \times 600 = 60 < 150E[repair cost]=0.10×600=60<150

Interpretation: On average the warranty costs more than it saves; it buys peace of mind, not expected value.

51. Risk of a two-asset mix

Scenario: An illustrative portfolio holds 60% in asset A (SD 20%) and 40% in asset B (SD 10%), with correlation 0.3. This is a calculation exercise, not investment advice. Concept: Variance of a weighted sum.

σp2=0.62(0.2)2+0.42(0.1)2+2(0.6)(0.4)(0.2)(0.1)(0.3)=0.0144+0.0016+0.00288=0.01888\sigma_p^2 = 0.6^2(0.2)^2 + 0.4^2(0.1)^2 + 2(0.6)(0.4)(0.2)(0.1)(0.3) = 0.0144 + 0.0016 + 0.00288 = 0.01888σp2​=0.62(0.2)2+0.42(0.1)2+2(0.6)(0.4)(0.2)(0.1)(0.3)=0.0144+0.0016+0.00288=0.01888 σp=0.01888≈13.7%\sigma_p = \sqrt{0.01888} \approx 13.7\%σp​=0.01888​≈13.7%

Interpretation: The mix is less volatile than the weighted average of SDs (16%) because the assets do not move perfectly together.

52. Uncertainty in a project schedule

Scenario: Three independent tasks have duration SDs of 2, 3 and 6 days. Concept: Variances of independent variables add.

σtotal=22+32+62=49=7 days\sigma_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{2^2 + 3^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{49} = 7 \text{ days}σtotal​=22+32+62​=49​=7 days

Interpretation: The total uncertainty is dominated by the most uncertain task.

53. Mixed-up coats at a party

Scenario: nnn guests' coats are returned at random. How many guests expect to get their own coat? Concept: Linearity of expectation with indicator variables.

Each guest gets their own coat with probability 1/n1/n1/n, so

E[matches]=n×1n=1E[\text{matches}] = n \times \frac{1}{n} = 1E[matches]=n×n1​=1

Interpretation: Whether there are 5 guests or 500, the expected number of correct returns is one.

54. Restaurant no-shows

Scenario: A restaurant has 80 reservations; suppose each no-shows independently with probability 0.10. Concept: Binomial expectation and spread.

E=80×0.10=8,σ=80×0.1×0.9≈2.68E = 80 \times 0.10 = 8, \qquad \sigma = \sqrt{80 \times 0.1 \times 0.9} \approx 2.68E=80×0.10=8,σ=80×0.1×0.9​≈2.68

Interpretation: Expect about 8 empty tables' worth of guests, give or take 3.

55. The casino's long-run take

Scenario: Players wager a total of $1,000,000 on red at American roulette. Concept: Law of large numbers applied to the house edge from example 49.

E[casino win]=238×1 000 000≈52 632E[\text{casino win}] = \frac{2}{38} \times 1\,000\,000 \approx 52\,632E[casino win]=382​×1000000≈52632

Interpretation: Individual sessions vary wildly, but across huge volumes the result settles near the expected value.

56. Waiting for a bus

Scenario: A bus comes every 10 minutes and you arrive at a random time. Concept: Continuous uniform distribution on [0,10][0, 10][0,10].

E[W]=0+102=5,σ=1012≈2.89E[W] = \frac{0 + 10}{2} = 5, \qquad \sigma = \frac{10}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 2.89E[W]=20+10​=5,σ=12​10​≈2.89

Interpretation: You wait 5 minutes on average, and waits under 2 minutes or over 8 are each a 20% chance.

57. Time between customer arrivals

Scenario: Suppose customers arrive randomly, on average every 4 minutes. What is the chance of a gap longer than 10 minutes? Concept: Exponential distribution, P(T>t)=e−t/μP(T > t) = e^{-t/\mu}P(T>t)=e−t/μ.

P(T>10)=e−10/4=e−2.5≈0.082P(T > 10) = e^{-10/4} = e^{-2.5} \approx 0.082P(T>10)=e−10/4=e−2.5≈0.082

Interpretation: About 8% of gaps exceed 10 minutes, and the exponential is memoryless: having waited 5 minutes does not make an arrival "due."

Descriptive statistics

Descriptive statistics summarize data: where its center is, how spread out it is, and what shape it has.

58. Mean versus median salary

Scenario: A small firm's ten annual salaries, in thousands of dollars, are 42, 45, 48, 50, 52, 55, 58, 60, 65 and 400. Concept: Sensitivity of the mean to outliers.

xˉ=87510=87.5,median=52+552=53.5\bar{x} = \frac{875}{10} = 87.5, \qquad \text{median} = \frac{52 + 55}{2} = 53.5xˉ=10875​=87.5,median=252+55​=53.5

Interpretation: The mean suggests a typical salary of $87,500, but nine of ten employees earn $65,000 or less; the median describes them better.

59. Which shoe size to stock most

Scenario: A store's last 12 sales were sizes 8, 9, 9, 10, 9, 7, 11, 9, 8, 10, 9, 8. Concept: Mode.

Size 9 appears five times, more than any other size, so the mode is 9.

Interpretation: For stocking decisions on categories, the mode answers "what is most common" directly.

60. Day-to-day temperature variation

Scenario: Five daily highs (°C) were 18, 21, 23, 19, 24. Concept: Sample standard deviation.

xˉ=21,s2=(−3)2+02+22+(−2)2+325−1=264=6.5,s≈2.55\bar{x} = 21, \qquad s^2 = \frac{(-3)^2 + 0^2 + 2^2 + (-2)^2 + 3^2}{5 - 1} = \frac{26}{4} = 6.5, \qquad s \approx 2.55xˉ=21,s2=5−1(−3)2+02+22+(−2)2+32​=426​=6.5,s≈2.55

Interpretation: A typical day differs from the average by about 2.5 °C. Dividing by n−1n - 1n−1 corrects for using the sample mean.

61. Spread of delivery times

Scenario: Eleven delivery times (minutes) were 12, 14, 15, 15, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 25, 41. Concept: Quartiles and interquartile range (IQR).

Using the median of each half (excluding the overall median of 18):

Q1=15,Q3=22,IQR=22−15=7Q_1 = 15, \qquad Q_3 = 22, \qquad \text{IQR} = 22 - 15 = 7Q1​=15,Q3​=22,IQR=22−15=7

Interpretation: The middle half of deliveries spans 7 minutes. Software may give slightly different quartiles because several quartile conventions exist.

62. Flagging an outlier

Scenario: Same delivery data. Concept: The 1.5 × IQR fence rule used in box plots.

upper fence=22+1.5×7=32.5,lower fence=15−1.5×7=4.5\text{upper fence} = 22 + 1.5 \times 7 = 32.5, \qquad \text{lower fence} = 15 - 1.5 \times 7 = 4.5upper fence=22+1.5×7=32.5,lower fence=15−1.5×7=4.5

Interpretation: The 41-minute delivery is flagged for review; an outlier is a question, not automatically an error.

63. Comparing variability on different scales

Scenario: Machine A fills 500 g bags with SD 5 g; machine B fills 50 g bags with SD 1 g. Concept: Coefficient of variation, CV=s/xˉCV = s / \bar{x}CV=s/xˉ.

CVA=5500=1%,CVB=150=2%CV_A = \frac{5}{500} = 1\%, \qquad CV_B = \frac{1}{50} = 2\%CVA​=5005​=1%,CVB​=501​=2%

Interpretation: B has the smaller SD but is relatively twice as variable.

64. Weighted course grade

Scenario: Homework counts 20% (score 90), the midterm 30% (75) and the final 50% (82). Concept: Weighted mean.

0.2(90)+0.3(75)+0.5(82)=18+22.5+41=81.50.2(90) + 0.3(75) + 0.5(82) = 18 + 22.5 + 41 = 81.50.2(90)+0.3(75)+0.5(82)=18+22.5+41=81.5

Interpretation: The final exam's weight pulls the grade toward 82.

65. Average growth rate

Scenario: An investment gains 50% one year and loses 50% the next. Concept: Geometric mean for growth rates.

1.5×0.5=0.75,0.75≈0.866  ⇒  −13.4% per year1.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75, \qquad \sqrt{0.75} \approx 0.866 \;\Rightarrow\; -13.4\% \text{ per year}1.5×0.5=0.75,0.75​≈0.866⇒−13.4% per year

Interpretation: The arithmetic average return is 0%, yet the money shrank by 25%; compounding needs the geometric mean.

66. Average speed on a round trip

Scenario: You drive to a town at 60 km/h and return the same distance at 40 km/h. Concept: Harmonic mean for rates over equal distances.

vˉ=2160+140=48 km/h\bar{v} = \frac{2}{\frac{1}{60} + \frac{1}{40}} = 48 \text{ km/h}vˉ=601​+401​2​=48 km/h

Interpretation: The answer is not 50, because you spend more time at the slower speed.

67. Smoothing daily sales

Scenario: Daily sales were 120, 135, 128, 150, 160, 145. Concept: Three-day moving average.

120+135+1283≈127.7,135+128+1503≈137.7,128+150+1603=146,150+160+1453≈151.7\frac{120 + 135 + 128}{3} \approx 127.7, \quad \frac{135 + 128 + 150}{3} \approx 137.7, \quad \frac{128 + 150 + 160}{3} = 146, \quad \frac{150 + 160 + 145}{3} \approx 151.73120+135+128​≈127.7,3135+128+150​≈137.7,3128+150+160​=146,3150+160+145​≈151.7

Interpretation: The smoothed series shows a steady upward trend that day-to-day noise partly hides.

68. A guarantee that works for any distribution

Scenario: Wait times have mean 10 minutes and SD 2, but the shape is unknown. Concept: Chebyshev's inequality, at least 1−1/k21 - 1/k^21−1/k2 of values lie within kkk SDs.

k=2:  1−14=75% within [6,14],k=3:  1−19≈88.9%k = 2: \; 1 - \frac{1}{4} = 75\% \text{ within } [6, 14], \qquad k = 3: \; 1 - \frac{1}{9} \approx 88.9\%k=2:1−41​=75% within [6,14],k=3:1−91​≈88.9%

Interpretation: Without assuming normality you still get a guaranteed (if conservative) bound.

Sampling and confidence intervals

The standard error of the mean, σ/n\sigma/\sqrt{n}σ/n​, measures how much sample means vary from sample to sample. A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the true value in about 95% of repeated samples; any single interval either contains it or does not (NIST section 1.3.5.2).

69. Standard error of light bulb lifetimes

Scenario: A sample of 100 bulbs has SD 120 hours. Concept: Standard error.

SE=sn=120100=12 hoursSE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{120}{\sqrt{100}} = 12 \text{ hours}SE=n​s​=100​120​=12 hours

Interpretation: Individual bulbs vary by about 120 hours, but the sample average is uncertain by only about 12.

70. Confidence interval for average screen time

Scenario: A sample of 25 people reports a mean of 4.2 hours of daily screen time with SD 0.8. Concept: t-interval, xˉ±t0.975, n−1 s/n\bar{x} \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt{n}xˉ±t0.975,n−1​s/n​.

t0.975, 24≈2.064,2.064×0.825≈0.330t_{0.975,\,24} \approx 2.064, \qquad 2.064 \times \frac{0.8}{\sqrt{25}} \approx 0.330t0.975,24​≈2.064,2.064×25​0.8​≈0.330 4.2±0.33=[3.87,  4.53]4.2 \pm 0.33 = [3.87, \; 4.53]4.2±0.33=[3.87,4.53]

Interpretation: The data are consistent with a population average between about 3.9 and 4.5 hours.

71. Margin of error in an election poll

Scenario: A random sample of 1,000 voters shows 52% support for a candidate. Concept: Confidence interval for a proportion.

SE=0.52×0.481000≈0.0158,1.96×0.0158≈0.031SE = \sqrt{\frac{0.52 \times 0.48}{1000}} \approx 0.0158, \qquad 1.96 \times 0.0158 \approx 0.031SE=10000.52×0.48​​≈0.0158,1.96×0.0158≈0.031 0.52±0.031=[0.489,  0.551]0.52 \pm 0.031 = [0.489, \; 0.551]0.52±0.031=[0.489,0.551]

Interpretation: The interval includes values below 50%, so the poll alone cannot say the candidate leads.

72. How many people to survey

Scenario: A pollster wants a ±3 percentage point margin at 95% confidence. Concept: Sample size for a proportion, using the worst case p=0.5p = 0.5p=0.5.

n=1.962×0.5×0.50.032≈1067.1  ⇒  1068n = \frac{1.96^2 \times 0.5 \times 0.5}{0.03^2} \approx 1067.1 \;\Rightarrow\; 1068n=0.0321.962×0.5×0.5​≈1067.1⇒1068

Interpretation: Roughly a thousand respondents buys a ±3 point margin for a simple random sample; always round up.

73. Sample size for a mean

Scenario: Suppose blood pressure readings have SD 15 mmHg and a study wants the mean within ±2 mmHg at 95% confidence. Concept: n=(zσ/E)2n = (z\sigma/E)^2n=(zσ/E)2.

n=(1.96×152)2=216.09  ⇒  217n = \left(\frac{1.96 \times 15}{2}\right)^2 = 216.09 \;\Rightarrow\; 217n=(21.96×15​)2=216.09⇒217

Interpretation: About 217 participants are needed, before allowing for dropouts.

74. The cost of halving the margin of error

Scenario: The pollster from example 72 now wants ±1.5 points. Concept: Margin of error shrinks with n\sqrt{n}n​.

n=1.962×0.250.0152≈4268.4  ⇒  4269n = \frac{1.96^2 \times 0.25}{0.015^2} \approx 4268.4 \;\Rightarrow\; 4269n=0.01521.962×0.25​≈4268.4⇒4269

Interpretation: Twice the precision needs four times the sample, which is why precision gets expensive.

75. Surveying a large share of a small population

Scenario: A company surveys 400 of its 2,000 employees. Concept: Finite population correction (FPC).

FPC=N−nN−1=16001999≈0.895\text{FPC} = \sqrt{\frac{N - n}{N - 1}} = \sqrt{\frac{1600}{1999}} \approx 0.895FPC=N−1N−n​​=19991600​​≈0.895

Interpretation: Standard errors shrink by about 10.5% because a fifth of the whole population was sampled.

76. Stratified sampling by department

Scenario: A firm has 600 engineers, 300 salespeople and 100 support staff, and wants a sample of 200. Concept: Proportional allocation.

200×6001000=120,200×3001000=60,200×1001000=20200 \times \frac{600}{1000} = 120, \qquad 200 \times \frac{300}{1000} = 60, \qquad 200 \times \frac{100}{1000} = 20200×1000600​=120,200×1000300​=60,200×1000100​=20

Interpretation: Each group appears in the sample in its true proportion, so a small group cannot be missed by chance.

77. Averages are steadier than individuals

Scenario: Suppose individual delivery times have mean 30 and SD 6 minutes. A courier's daily average over 36 deliveries is reported. Concept: Central limit theorem.

SE=636=1,P(Xˉ>32)=P(Z>2)≈0.0228SE = \frac{6}{\sqrt{36}} = 1, \qquad P(\bar{X} > 32) = P(Z > 2) \approx 0.0228SE=36​6​=1,P(Xˉ>32)=P(Z>2)≈0.0228

Interpretation: A 32-minute single delivery is ordinary, but a 32-minute daily average is rare.

78. Estimating a fish population

Scenario: Ecologists tag 100 fish and release them. Later they catch 80, of which 16 are tagged. Concept: Capture–recapture (Lincoln–Petersen estimator).

N^=100×8016=500\hat{N} = \frac{100 \times 80}{16} = 500N^=16100×80​=500

A bias-reduced version (Chapman's estimator), (101)(81)17−1\frac{(101)(81)}{17} - 117(101)(81)​−1, gives about 480.

Interpretation: The lake holds roughly 500 fish, assuming tagged fish mix evenly and are not easier or harder to catch.

Hypothesis testing and A/B tests

A hypothesis test asks how surprising the data would be if a default claim (the null hypothesis, H0H_0H0​) were true. The p-value measures that surprise; as the American Statistical Association's 2016 statement stresses, it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true and does not measure the size of an effect (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).

79. Are cereal boxes underfilled?

Scenario: Boxes should hold 500 g. Suppose the filling SD is known to be 10 g, and 40 boxes average 497 g. Concept: One-sample z-test.

z=497−50010/40=−31.581≈−1.90,ptwo-sided≈0.058z = \frac{497 - 500}{10/\sqrt{40}} = \frac{-3}{1.581} \approx -1.90, \qquad p_{\text{two-sided}} \approx 0.058z=10/40​497−500​=1.581−3​≈−1.90,ptwo-sided​≈0.058

Interpretation: At the 5% level the shortfall is not statistically significant; it is not proof that filling is fine either.

80. Testing a battery-life claim

Scenario: A maker claims 20 hours of battery life. Sixteen tested units average 19.2 hours with SD 1.6. Concept: One-sample t-test, one-sided.

t=19.2−201.6/16=−0.80.4=−2.0,df=15,p≈0.032t = \frac{19.2 - 20}{1.6/\sqrt{16}} = \frac{-0.8}{0.4} = -2.0, \qquad df = 15, \qquad p \approx 0.032t=1.6/16​19.2−20​=0.4−0.8​=−2.0,df=15,p≈0.032

Interpretation: If the claim were true, an average this low would happen only about 3% of the time.

81. An A/B test on a sign-up button

Scenario: Version A converts 200 of 4,000 visitors (5.00%); version B converts 250 of 4,000 (6.25%). Concept: Two-proportion z-test.

p^=4508000=0.05625,SE=0.05625×0.94375×(14000+14000)≈0.00515\hat{p} = \frac{450}{8000} = 0.05625, \qquad SE = \sqrt{0.05625 \times 0.94375 \times \left(\frac{1}{4000} + \frac{1}{4000}\right)} \approx 0.00515p^​=8000450​=0.05625,SE=0.05625×0.94375×(40001​+40001​)​≈0.00515 z=0.0625−0.05000.00515≈2.43,p≈0.015z = \frac{0.0625 - 0.0500}{0.00515} \approx 2.43, \qquad p \approx 0.015z=0.005150.0625−0.0500​≈2.43,p≈0.015

Interpretation: The lift is unlikely to be pure chance, assuming the test was planned in advance and not stopped early when it looked good.

82. Is the die fair?

Scenario: A die rolled 60 times shows faces 1–6 with counts 8, 9, 12, 11, 6, 14. Concept: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test, each expected count 10.

χ2=∑(O−E)2E=4+1+4+1+16+1610=4.2,df=5,p≈0.52\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E} = \frac{4 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 16 + 16}{10} = 4.2, \qquad df = 5, \qquad p \approx 0.52χ2=∑E(O−E)2​=104+1+4+1+16+16​=4.2,df=5,p≈0.52

Interpretation: These counts are entirely typical for a fair die; uneven-looking counts are normal in small samples.

83. Remote-work preference by department

Scenario: In a survey, 60 of 100 engineers and 35 of 100 salespeople prefer remote work. Concept: Chi-square test of independence.

Expected counts under independence are 47.5 (remote) and 52.5 (office) in each department:

χ2=2[(60−47.5)247.5+(40−52.5)252.5]≈12.53,df=1,p≈0.0004\chi^2 = 2\left[\frac{(60 - 47.5)^2}{47.5} + \frac{(40 - 52.5)^2}{52.5}\right] \approx 12.53, \qquad df = 1, \qquad p \approx 0.0004χ2=2[47.5(60−47.5)2​+52.5(40−52.5)2​]≈12.53,df=1,p≈0.0004

Interpretation: Preference is strongly associated with department in this sample.

84. Comparing two teaching methods

Scenario: Method A: 30 students, mean 78, SD 10. Method B: 30 students, mean 72, SD 12. Concept: Welch two-sample t-test (NIST section 1.3.5.3).

SE=10230+12230≈2.852,t=78−722.852≈2.10SE = \sqrt{\frac{10^2}{30} + \frac{12^2}{30}} \approx 2.852, \qquad t = \frac{78 - 72}{2.852} \approx 2.10SE=30102​+30122​​≈2.852,t=2.85278−72​≈2.10

With Welch–Satterthwaite df≈56.2df \approx 56.2df≈56.2, the two-sided p≈0.040p \approx 0.040p≈0.040.

Interpretation: The difference is statistically significant at 5%, but only a randomized design would justify calling it an effect of the method.

85. Did training speed up typing?

Scenario: Eight employees' typing speed changed by +5, +3, +6, −1, +4, +2, +7, +3 words per minute after training. Concept: Paired t-test on the differences.

dˉ=3.625,sd≈2.504,t=3.6252.504/8≈4.10,df=7,p≈0.005\bar{d} = 3.625, \qquad s_d \approx 2.504, \qquad t = \frac{3.625}{2.504/\sqrt{8}} \approx 4.10, \qquad df = 7, \qquad p \approx 0.005dˉ=3.625,sd​≈2.504,t=2.504/8​3.625​≈4.10,df=7,p≈0.005

Interpretation: Pairing removes person-to-person variation, which makes a small study informative.

86. Running twenty tests at once

Scenario: An analyst tests 20 metrics, each at α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05, when nothing has really changed. Concept: Family-wise error rate and the Bonferroni correction.

P(at least one false positive)=1−0.9520≈0.642,αBonferroni=0.0520=0.0025P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.642, \qquad \alpha_{\text{Bonferroni}} = \frac{0.05}{20} = 0.0025P(at least one false positive)=1−0.9520≈0.642,αBonferroni​=200.05​=0.0025

Interpretation: Test enough things and something will look "significant"; adjust the threshold or pre-register the main metric.

87. How long to run an A/B test

Scenario: The baseline conversion rate is 5%, and the team wants to detect a lift to 6% with 5% significance (two-sided) and 80% power. Concept: Sample size for two proportions.

n=(1.962(0.055)(0.945)+0.84160.05(0.95)+0.06(0.94))2(0.06−0.05)2≈8158n = \frac{\left(1.96\sqrt{2(0.055)(0.945)} + 0.8416\sqrt{0.05(0.95) + 0.06(0.94)}\right)^2}{(0.06 - 0.05)^2} \approx 8158n=(0.06−0.05)2(1.962(0.055)(0.945)​+0.84160.05(0.95)+0.06(0.94)​)2​≈8158

Interpretation: About 8,158 visitors per variant are needed; small lifts on small baselines need large samples.

88. The power of the cereal-box test

Scenario: Return to example 79. If the true mean really is 497 g, how often would that test detect it? Concept: Statistical power.

With the standardized shift δ=−1.897\delta = -1.897δ=−1.897 and a two-sided cutoff of 1.96:

power=Φ(−1.96−δ)+Φ(−1.96+δ)=Φ(−0.063)+Φ(−3.857)≈0.475\text{power} = \Phi(-1.96 - \delta) + \Phi(-1.96 + \delta) = \Phi(-0.063) + \Phi(-3.857) \approx 0.475power=Φ(−1.96−δ)+Φ(−1.96+δ)=Φ(−0.063)+Φ(−3.857)≈0.475

Interpretation: The test misses a real 3 g shortfall more than half the time, so "not significant" in example 79 was weak reassurance.

Correlation and regression

The next four examples share one small, illustrative data set: monthly advertising spend xxx (in $1,000s) of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and sales yyy (in $10,000s) of 3, 5, 4, 7, 8. Its building blocks are xˉ=3\bar{x} = 3xˉ=3, yˉ=5.4\bar{y} = 5.4yˉ​=5.4, Sxx=10S_{xx} = 10Sxx​=10, Syy=17.2S_{yy} = 17.2Syy​=17.2 and Sxy=12S_{xy} = 12Sxy​=12.

89. Correlation between advertising and sales

Scenario: Does sales move with advertising? Concept: Pearson correlation coefficient.

r=SxySxxSyy=1210×17.2≈0.915r = \frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} S_{yy}}} = \frac{12}{\sqrt{10 \times 17.2}} \approx 0.915r=Sxx​Syy​​Sxy​​=10×17.2​12​≈0.915

Interpretation: A strong positive linear association; it does not by itself show that advertising causes sales.

90. Fitting a regression line

Scenario: Same data; predict sales at a spend of 6. Concept: Least-squares line, b=Sxy/Sxxb = S_{xy}/S_{xx}b=Sxy​/Sxx​, a=yˉ−bxˉa = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}a=yˉ​−bxˉ.

b=1210=1.2,a=5.4−1.2×3=1.8,y^=1.8+1.2xb = \frac{12}{10} = 1.2, \qquad a = 5.4 - 1.2 \times 3 = 1.8, \qquad \hat{y} = 1.8 + 1.2xb=1012​=1.2,a=5.4−1.2×3=1.8,y^​=1.8+1.2x y^(6)=1.8+7.2=9.0\hat{y}(6) = 1.8 + 7.2 = 9.0y^​(6)=1.8+7.2=9.0

Interpretation: Each extra $1,000 is associated with $12,000 more sales, but x=6x = 6x=6 is outside the data, so this is a cautious extrapolation.

91. How much does the line explain?

Scenario: Same data. Concept: Coefficient of determination.

R2=r2≈0.9152≈0.837R^2 = r^2 \approx 0.915^2 \approx 0.837R2=r2≈0.9152≈0.837

Interpretation: About 84% of the month-to-month variation in sales is accounted for by the linear relationship with spend.

92. Residuals and typical prediction error

Scenario: Same data. Concept: Residuals y−y^y - \hat{y}y−y^​ and the standard error of the estimate.

Predicted values are 3.0, 4.2, 5.4, 6.6, 7.8, so the residuals are 0, 0.8, −1.4, 0.4, 0.2:

SSE=0+0.64+1.96+0.16+0.04=2.8,se=2.85−2≈0.966SSE = 0 + 0.64 + 1.96 + 0.16 + 0.04 = 2.8, \qquad s_e = \sqrt{\frac{2.8}{5 - 2}} \approx 0.966SSE=0+0.64+1.96+0.16+0.04=2.8,se​=5−22.8​​≈0.966

Interpretation: Predictions are typically off by about 1 unit ($10,000); month 3 is the worst fit.

93. Interpreting a slope in house prices

Scenario: Suppose a regression of price on floor area gives a slope of $150 per square foot. Two otherwise similar houses differ by 200 square feet. Concept: Slope as a rate of change.

150×200=30 000150 \times 200 = 30\,000150×200=30000

Interpretation: The model predicts a $30,000 price difference, holding the model's other inputs fixed; it is a prediction, not an appraisal.

94. Ice cream and swimming accidents

Scenario: Suppose ice cream sales (XXX) and swimming accidents (YYY) correlate at 0.6, while each correlates with temperature (ZZZ) at 0.8 and 0.75. Concept: Partial correlation controls for a confounder.

rXY⋅Z=rXY−rXZrYZ(1−rXZ2)(1−rYZ2)=0.6−0.8×0.750.36×0.4375=00.397=0r_{XY \cdot Z} = \frac{r_{XY} - r_{XZ} r_{YZ}}{\sqrt{(1 - r_{XZ}^2)(1 - r_{YZ}^2)}} = \frac{0.6 - 0.8 \times 0.75}{\sqrt{0.36 \times 0.4375}} = \frac{0}{0.397} = 0rXY⋅Z​=(1−rXZ2​)(1−rYZ2​)​rXY​−rXZ​rYZ​​=0.36×0.4375​0.6−0.8×0.75​=0.3970​=0

Interpretation: In this constructed example, the whole association is explained by hot weather. Correlation is not causation.

95. Regression to the mean in performance reviews

Scenario: Suppose scores on two quarterly reviews correlate at r=0.5r = 0.5r=0.5, and an employee scored 2 SDs above average last quarter. Concept: Regression to the mean, z^y=r zx\hat{z}_y = r\,z_xz^y​=rzx​.

z^y=0.5×2=1\hat{z}_y = 0.5 \times 2 = 1z^y​=0.5×2=1

Interpretation: The best prediction is still above average but closer to the mean, with no change in ability required; praise or criticism given in between can easily be mistaken for the cause.

Paradoxes and pitfalls

96. Berkeley admissions and Simpson's paradox

Scenario: In 1973, graduate admissions at the University of California, Berkeley appeared to favor men. The data below are the six largest departments, as published with Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell (1975) and distributed as R's UCBAdmissions data set. Concept: Simpson's paradox, where a trend in every group reverses or disappears when groups are combined.

Combined over the six departments:

men: 11982691≈44.5%,women: 5571835≈30.4%\text{men: } \frac{1198}{2691} \approx 44.5\%, \qquad \text{women: } \frac{557}{1835} \approx 30.4\%men: 26911198​≈44.5%,women: 1835557​≈30.4%

By department:

Department Men applied Men admitted Women applied Women admitted
A 825 62.1% 108 82.4%
B 560 63.0% 25 68.0%
C 325 36.9% 593 34.1%
D 417 33.1% 375 34.9%
E 191 27.7% 393 23.9%
F 373 5.9% 341 7.0%

Women had the higher admission rate in four of the six departments. Most women applied to departments C–F, which admitted few applicants of either sex, while most men applied to A and B, which admitted most applicants.

Interpretation: The aggregate gap reflects where people applied, which matches the original authors' conclusion that the data did not show department-level bias against women. Always ask whether a lurking grouping variable explains a combined trend.

97. The gambler's fallacy

Scenario: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. What is the chance the next flip is heads? Concept: Independence.

P(heads on flip 6∣5 heads)=0.5,P(6 heads in a row, before starting)=0.56=164P(\text{heads on flip 6} \mid 5 \text{ heads}) = 0.5, \qquad P(6 \text{ heads in a row, before starting}) = 0.5^6 = \frac{1}{64}P(heads on flip 6∣5 heads)=0.5,P(6 heads in a row, before starting)=0.56=641​

Interpretation: A streak is unlikely in advance, but once five heads have happened, the coin has no memory.

98. Benford's law for leading digits

Scenario: An analyst checks whether the first digits of thousands of invoice amounts look natural. Concept: Benford's law, P(d)=log⁡10(1+1/d)P(d) = \log_{10}(1 + 1/d)P(d)=log10​(1+1/d), which applies to many data sets spanning several orders of magnitude.

P(1)=log⁡102≈0.301,P(9)=log⁡10109≈0.046P(1) = \log_{10} 2 \approx 0.301, \qquad P(9) = \log_{10}\frac{10}{9} \approx 0.046P(1)=log10​2≈0.301,P(9)=log10​910​≈0.046

Interpretation: Under Benford's law, about 30% of amounts would start with 1 and under 5% with 9. A large deviation is a reason to look closer, not proof of fraud, since many legitimate data sets do not follow the law.

99. The class-size paradox

Scenario: A school has two classes, one with 10 students and one with 90. Concept: The inspection paradox: averages depend on who is asked.

average per class=10+902=50,average experienced by a student=102+902100=82\text{average per class} = \frac{10 + 90}{2} = 50, \qquad \text{average experienced by a student} = \frac{10^2 + 90^2}{100} = 82average per class=210+90​=50,average experienced by a student=100102+902​=82

Interpretation: The school can truthfully report 50 while the typical student sits in a class of 90. The same effect can make buses or gyms feel more crowded than their reported averages.

100. Small hospitals and extreme days

Scenario: One hospital has about 15 births a day, another about 45. Which records more days on which over 60% of babies are boys? Assume each birth is a boy with probability 0.5. Concept: Small samples vary more (the binomial spread shrinks with nnn).

"Over 60%" means at least 10 of 15, or at least 28 of 45:

P(X≥10∣n=15)≈0.151,P(X≥28∣n=45)≈0.068P(X \ge 10 \mid n = 15) \approx 0.151, \qquad P(X \ge 28 \mid n = 45) \approx 0.068P(X≥10∣n=15)≈0.151,P(X≥28∣n=45)≈0.068

Interpretation: The small hospital sees such days more than twice as often. Extreme rates, good or bad, cluster in small groups, so rank small schools, towns or stores with care.

Common mistakes

These are the errors that show up again and again when the examples above are applied to real data:

  • Ignoring the base rate. Examples 13, 16 and 22 show that an accurate test for a rare event still produces mostly false alarms. Always ask how common the thing is before interpreting a positive.
  • Reversing a conditional probability. P(A∣B)P(A \mid B)P(A∣B) and P(B∣A)P(B \mid A)P(B∣A) answer different questions (examples 17 and 23).
  • Assuming independence that is not there. Redundant systems (example 8) and repeated tests (example 14) only behave as calculated if their failures are unrelated.
  • Adding standard deviations. Variances of independent quantities add; standard deviations do not (examples 44 and 52).
  • Using the mean for skewed data. For incomes, house prices and wait times, report the median as well (example 58).
  • Misreading a confidence interval. The 95% describes how often the method succeeds over repeated samples, not the probability that one computed interval is correct (NIST section 1.3.5.2).
  • Treating p < 0.05 as a verdict. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about effect size (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016). "Not significant" can simply mean low power (example 88).
  • Testing many things and reporting the winner. Multiple comparisons inflate false positives quickly (example 86). Decide the main metric and sample size before an A/B test starts (example 87).
  • Equating correlation with causation. A lurking variable can create or erase an association (examples 94 and 96).
  • Expecting streaks to correct themselves. Independent events have no memory (examples 57 and 97).
  • Over-reading small samples. The most extreme results usually come from the smallest groups (example 100).

Next steps

To keep practicing, pair these examples with the other guides in this series:

  • Math formulas every student should know, a reference for the formulas used above.
  • Math tricks to solve problems faster, for quicker mental arithmetic on percentages and fractions.
  • Algebra problems with solutions for beginners, if rearranging formulas such as the sample-size equations felt shaky.
  • Linear algebra concepts for machine learning, the natural next step after regression.

You can also browse more mathematics writing in the Mathematics category.

  2. NIST/SEMATECH. e-Handbook of Statistical Methods (last updated 2022). National Institute of Standards and Technology. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/ (doi:10.18434/M32189). Sections used: 1.3.5.2 Confidence Limits for the Mean, 1.3.5.3 Two-Sample t-Test for Equal Means, 1.3.6.6.1 Normal Distribution, 6.1.6 What is Process Capability?.

title: How to Read an Engineering Blog Post Critically
description: A practical checklist for separating transferable lessons from context-specific stories when reading architecture and scalability write-ups from large tech companies.
author: BlogAI Editors

toc.text: Start with the problem, not the solution
Separate the claim from the evidence
Map it to your own constraints

html:
Company engineering blogs are some of the most useful public writing about real systems. They are also written by teams with a specific scale, budget, history, and set of constraints that are rarely spelled out. Reading them well means asking which parts of the story would survive in your own environment.

Start with the problem, not the solution

Before judging the architecture, write down the problem in one sentence. A post about rebuilding a message queue makes sense only once you know whether the pain was throughput, operational cost, ordering guarantees, or team ownership.

If you cannot state the problem after reading the introduction, the post is probably describing a solution looking for a justification, and the lessons will be hard to transfer.

Find the numbers that matter

Scale changes which designs are reasonable. Look for:

  • Request or event volume, ideally with peak and average figures.
  • Data size and how fast it grows.
  • Latency targets and which percentile they refer to.
  • Team size that builds and operates the system.

When these are missing, treat performance claims as directional rather than as evidence you can plan around.

Separate the claim from the evidence

A useful habit is to keep a two-column note while reading:

The post claims The evidence shown
"Migration cut latency in half" A before/after chart, but no load figures
"The new design is simpler" Fewer services, but a new dependency
"No downtime during rollout" A described dual-write strategy

Claims with concrete evidence are the ones worth citing in your own design reviews.

Look for what went wrong

The most transferable sections are often the incidents, rollbacks, and abandoned approaches. A post that lists only successes is either very short on detail or leaving out the part you most need. Pay attention to phrases like "we initially tried" or "in hindsight": they usually introduce the real lesson.

Map it to your own constraints

Finally, check the design against what you actually have:

  1. Do you have the same failure modes, or are you solving a problem you do not have yet?
  2. Could your team operate the extra components on call?
  3. What is the smallest version of this idea that would help today?

A quick worked example

Suppose a post describes sharding a database by customer ID to handle growth. The transferable idea is partitioning by the key most queries already filter on. The non-transferable part may be the custom routing layer, which was only needed because of thousands of shards. At smaller scale, built-in partitioning in your existing database may give you the same benefit.

Further reading

The Engineering category collects blogs that publish this kind of write-up regularly. If you want them in one place, follow them with a feed reader as described in How to Follow Technical Blogs with RSS and OPML.

title: How to Follow Technical Blogs with RSS and OPML
description: Set up a feed reader, import the BlogAI OPML file, and build a reading routine that keeps you current without endless tabs or algorithmic timelines.
author: BlogAI Editors

toc.text: What RSS and OPML actually are

html:
Most of the best technical writing on the web still lives on independent blogs. Their authors publish when they have something worth saying, which is exactly why checking them by hand does not work: you visit ten sites, nine have nothing new, and you stop visiting. RSS solves this by letting the blogs come to you.

What RSS and OPML actually are

RSS (and its close relative Atom) is a small XML file a website publishes alongside its pages. Each entry lists a post's title, link, date, and usually a summary. A feed reader polls these files and shows you only what is new.

OPML is a list of feeds. It is how you move a whole set of subscriptions between readers in one step. A minimal OPML file looks like this:

<opml version="2.0">
  <head><title>My Feeds</title></head>
  <body>
    <outline text="Engineering">
      <outline type="rss" text="Example Blog"
               xmlUrl="https://example.com/feed.xml"
               htmlUrl="https://example.com" />
    </outline>
  </body>
</opml>

Each nested outline becomes a folder in most readers, so the categories in a well-made OPML file carry straight over into your reader.

Step 1: Choose a feed reader

Any reader that can import OPML will work. When comparing them, these are the features that matter for technical reading:

Feature Why it matters
OPML import and export Lets you start from a curated list and leave without lock-in
Folders or tags Keeps engineering, maths, and science feeds separate
Full-text view Long posts are easier to read without the site's layout
Keyboard shortcuts Triage fifty items in a few minutes
Sync across devices Read on the phone, save for the desk

Self-hosted readers are a good option if you already run a home server; hosted readers are simpler if you do not.

Step 2: Import the BlogAI collection

  1. Download the BlogAI OPML file. It contains every blog in the community directory that publishes a feed, grouped by category.
  2. In your reader, find the import option (usually under settings or subscriptions) and choose the downloaded file.
  3. Delete the folders you do not care about. A smaller list you actually read beats a large one you ignore.

You can also subscribe to a single blog: every listing in the directory with a feed shows an RSS button that copies or opens its feed URL.

Step 3: Build a reading routine

Feeds only help if you have a habit for clearing them:

  • Triage, then read. Skim headlines once a day and save only what is worth a full read.
  • Separate fast and slow feeds. News-style sites post daily; personal blogs post monthly. Put them in different folders so the slow, high-signal posts are not buried.
  • Mark all as read without guilt. If a folder overflows after a holiday, clear it. The important posts will be referenced again.

Troubleshooting common feed problems

The site has no feed link. Try common paths such as /feed, /rss, /feed.xml, or /atom.xml. Many readers also discover feeds automatically when you paste the site's home page URL.

The feed only shows summaries. That is the publisher's choice. Use your reader's full-text option if it has one, or open the post in the browser.

A feed stopped updating. Sites move platforms and feed URLs change. Check the site's footer for a new feed link, and if a directory listing is out of date, submit a correction.

Where to go next

Browse the Engineering category for systems and infrastructure writing, or explore the full blog directory by topic.
